Agreement: If any correct process decides a value v, then no correct process validates or decides any value v^{\prime } \ne v.

Integrity: No correct process decides or receives a \mathsf {completed} indication unless it has previously proposed.

Termination: If all correct processes propose and no correct process abandons Crux, then every correct process eventually receives a \mathsf {completed} indication.

Totality: If any correct process receives a \mathsf {completed} indication at some time \tau , then every correct process validates a value by time \max (\tau , \text{GST}) + 2\delta .

Synchronicity: Let \tau denote the first time a correct process proposes to Crux.
If (1) \tau \ge \text{GST}, (2) all correct processes propose by time \tau + \Delta _{\mathit {shift}}, and (3) no correct process abandons Crux by time \tau + \Delta _{\mathit {total}}, then every correct process decides by time \tau + \Delta _{\mathit {total}}.

Completion time: If a correct process p_i proposes to Crux at some time \tau \ge \text{GST}, then p_i does not receive a \mathsf {completed} indication by time \tau + \Delta _{\mathit {total}}.

In brief, Crux guarantees safety of Repeater always (even if Crux is run before GST), and it ensures liveness of Repeater (by guaranteeing synchronicity) only after GST (assuming that all correct processes are “\Delta _{\mathit {shift}}-synchronized”).
We underline that a correct process can validate a value from Crux even if (1) it has not previously proposed, or (2) it has previously abandoned Crux, or (3) it has previously received a \mathsf {completed} indication.

input: How do query and key noise, as well as signal dynamics, influence each other across different intervals, specifically [T2, T3+] and [T4-, T4+]?
expected_output:
The query and key noise, as well as signal dynamics, influence each other across different intervals, specifically [T2, T3+] and [T4-, T4+], in the following ways. For the interval [T2, T3+], the query/key noise dynamics remain unchanged, and the query/key signal dynamics are dominated by the sign of the summation of query/key noise. According to Lemma 10.9, the query and key noise update rules are given by the equations for the dot products of the weight vectors with the input vectors, which depend on the sign of the current dot product and the norm of the input vector. Additionally, the absolute values of the dot products are bounded by multiples of the time step, the learning rate, and the standard deviation of the noise. 

In the interval [T4-, T4+], the behavior of the query and key noise, as well as the signal dynamics, changes. For those samples where the query/key noise aligns with the query/key signal, the query/key noise dynamics remain unchanged. However, for those samples where the query/key noise does not align with the query/key signal, the query noise dynamics remain unchanged, while the key noise starts to decrease but remains greater than zero at T4+. The time T4+ is defined as the first time the condition involving the dot products of the weight vectors with the input vectors and the mean vector is met, which implies that T4+ is greater than or equal to T4-. At T4+, the sum of the products of certain terms and the dot products of the weight vectors with the input vectors is less than the sum of the products of other terms and the dot products of the weight vectors with the mean vector, indicating a specific relationship between the query/key noise and signal dynamics.

input: What are the advantages of using high-energy neutrino beams in enhancing precision in electroweak measurements?
expected_output: The use of high-energy neutrino beams in precision electroweak measurements offers several advantages, as discussed in the article "Precision Measurements with High Energy Neutrino Beams" by J. M. Conrad, M. H. Shaevitz, and T. Bolton, published in the Review of Modern Physics in 1998. High-energy neutrino beams provide a unique opportunity to study electroweak interactions with high precision, allowing for precise measurements of fundamental parameters such as the weak mixing angle and the mass of the W boson. The high energy of the neutrino beams enables the production of a large number of neutrino interactions, which can be used to reduce statistical uncertainties and increase the precision of the measurements. Additionally, the use of neutrino beams allows for the study of electroweak interactions in a clean and well-defined environment, with minimal backgrounds and systematic uncertainties. Overall, the advantages of using high-energy neutrino beams in precision electroweak measurements include high precision, high statistics, and a well-controlled experimental environment, making them a powerful tool for studying the electroweak interactions and testing the Standard Model of particle physics.

input: Does ES+RL convergence outperform standard RL in complex environments, and what are the key advantages and limitations of this approach?
expected_output: The proposed approach of combining Evolutionary Search (ES) with standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) has the potential to outperform standard RL in complex environments. The key advantages of this approach, as seen in the Evolutionary Operators for Reinforcement Learning (EORL) algorithm, include improved convergence to the globally optimal policy, simplicity of implementation, and reduced environment interactions. Additionally, the introduction of Evolutionary Operators allows for large search steps in the policy space, enabling exploration of promising regions. The existence of multiple policies also leads to more stable convergence compared to single-policy RL. However, the limitations of this approach include the need for careful tuning of hyperparameters and the potential for increased computational complexity. Overall, the ES+RL approach offers a promising solution for improving the convergence and stability of RL in complex environments, but its effectiveness depends on the specific problem and implementation details.
context: Reinforcement learning (RL) has always faced challenges with stable learning and convergence, given its reliance on a scalar reward signal and its propensity to reach local optima . While tabular RL admits reasonable theoretical analysis, there are very few guarantees in the case of Deep RL. In this paper, we propose a novel way of combining Evolutionary Search (ES) with standard RL that improves the probability of converging to the globally optimal policy.

In this paper, we focus on methods and environments that do not require the massively parallel architectures of typical ES methods. We are likely to encounter such constraints wherever simulations are expensive or even unavailable for local compute (for example, physical environments or ones hosted on servers). Therefore we assume that only one policy is able to interact with the environment in one episode, in a serialised fashion. This has the added advantage of allowing us to compare serial and parallelised methods directly, in terms of sample complexity.We believe that the proposed algorithm (called Evolutionary Operators for Reinforcement Learning or EORL) has the following novel and useful characteristics. First, it is very simple to implement, and modifications to standard RL and ES algorithms are minimal. Second, it requires far fewer environment interactions than other RL+ES approaches. Specifically, only one policy interacts with the environment at a time, thus making EORL equivalent in sample complexity to standard RL approaches. Third, the existence of multiple policies allows the algorithm to have more stable convergence than single-policy RL. Fourth, the introduction of Evolutionary Operators gives us the ability to take large search steps in the policy space, and to explore regions that are already promising.The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Section describes the specific RL setting within which we discuss the proposed work. Section describes the methodology, while Section describes the experiments and results.

The second environment is adapted from Contrastive Experience Replay . We consider an m\times m grid, with the agent spawning at position [1,1] in each episode, and the goal state at position [m,m] as shown in Figure REF . There are 4 possible actions in each step, UP,DOWN,LEFT,RIGHT. An action which would take the agent outside the edge of the grid has no effect on the state. Multiple versions of the same task can be produced by varying the effect of the subgoals \mathcal {I}_1 and \mathcal {I}_2 located at [1,m] and [m,1] respectively. The variations are,Subgoal 0: In the most basic version, visiting either or both subgoals on the way to the goal has no effect. If \tau is the timeout defined for the task, the agent gets a reward of {-1}/{\tau } for every step that does not lead to a goal, and a terminal reward of +10 for reaching the goal. The grid size can be varied.Subgoal 1: The exploration task can be made more challenging by `activating' one subgoal, \mathcal {I}_1. The agent gets a terminal reward of +10 if it visits subgoal \mathcal {I}_1 at position [1,m] on the way to the goal, and a smaller terminal reward of +1 for going to the goal directly without visiting \mathcal {I}_1. The other subgoal \mathcal {I}_2 has no effect. Among the trajectories shown in Figure REF , the green and purple ones will get a terminal reward of +10, the blue one will get +1, while the red one gets no terminal reward.Subgoal 2+: In this case, both subgoals are activated. The agent gets a reward of +10 only if both \mathcal {I}_1 and \mathcal {I}_2 are visited on the way to the goal (regardless of order between them). A terminal reward of +2 is given for visiting only one subgoal on the way, and a reward of +1 is given for reaching the goal without visiting any subgoals (blue=+1, purple=+2, green=+10, red=0 in Figure REF ).Subgoal 2-: A final level of complexity is introduced by providing a negative reward for visiting only one subgoal. Specifically, the agent gets a reward of +10 only if both \mathcal {I}_1 and \mathcal {I}_2 are visited on the way to the goal (regardless of order between them). A terminal reward of -1 is given for visiting only one subgoal on the way, and a reward of +1 is given for reaching the goal without visiting any subgoals. Going to the goal directly has a better reward than visiting one subgoal on the way.All the algorithms in this version of the environment are trained on 10 random seeds, but with varying episode counts and decay rates based on complexity of the task. The timeout is set to 10 times the length of the optimal path. All the agents (except HER) use a fully connected feedforward network with an input of size 4 (consisting of normalised x and y position and binary flags indicating whether \mathcal {I}_1 and \mathcal {I}_2 respectively have been visited in the current episode), two hidden layers of size 32 and 8 respectively with ReLU activation, and a linear output layer of size 4. Since HER augments the input state with the intended goal, its input size is 8. Rewards are computed using Monte-Carlo backups.Introducing stochasticity: Finally, we create stochastic versions of each of the 2D environments by introducing different levels of randomness in the actions.

On the other hand, REACH_G is an equivalence relation defined on the Cartesian product of the graph language GL_G and the set of states S_G of the S-graph G. The key difference between GL_G and REACH_G is that GL_G is a language, whereas REACH_G is a relation that captures the reachability between different states and labels in the graph. Specifically, REACH_G relates pairs of elements from GL_G and S_G if they can be reached from each other through a sequence of transitions in the graph. In contrast, GL_G simply defines the set of valid labels or strings that can be associated with the graph, without considering the reachability between them.

input: What are the limitations of interval attractors in set operations and recovery, and how do these limitations impact their performance in practice?
expected_output: The limitations of interval attractors in set operations and recovery are primarily related to their definition and the conditions they must satisfy. Specifically, interval attractors in the subset Ψ_mRecover of set Ψ_RR must satisfy two conditions: (1) they must be in the recover function of an interval attractor in the subset Ψ_source, and (2) the recover function of that interval attractor must not intersect with the lex set of the attractor position. These limitations can impact the performance of interval attractors in practice, as they may not be able to capture all possible interval attractors in certain scenarios. Additionally, the expectations of the number of interval attractors, such as E[m_h] and E[m'_t], are bounded by O(H) and O(log n), respectively, which can also limit their performance. Furthermore, the condition Ψ_nRecover(λ) ∩ Ψ_nRecover(λ') = ∅ must hold, which can restrict the applicability of interval attractors in certain situations. Overall, these limitations highlight the need for careful consideration of the properties and conditions of interval attractors in set operations and recovery to ensure their effective performance in practice.

input: What is the impact of L_2 regularization on the robustness of classifiers against poisoning attacks?
expected_output: The impact of L_2 regularization on the robustness of classifiers against poisoning attacks is significant, as it reduces the effect of poisoning points on the decision boundary. When L_2 regularization is applied, the decision boundary shifts only slightly, even when a single poisoning point is injected, and the validation error remains relatively stable regardless of the position of the poisoning point. This is in contrast to non-regularized classifiers, where a single poisoning point can significantly alter the decision boundary and increase the validation error. The use of L_2 regularization makes the algorithm more stable and robust against poisoning attacks, and the importance of regularization increases in regions where the poisoning point can influence the classifier more.

input: Does BD-ΛCDM's modification of parameters actually improve the fit to observational data compared to standard models?
expected_output: The Brans-Dicke theory with a cosmological constant (BD-ΛCDM) modifies the parameters of the standard ΛCDM model, and this modification can potentially improve the fit to observational data. The introduction of the scalar field φ in BD-ΛCDM allows for a more flexible description of the universe's evolution, particularly in the early stages. The effective equation of state (EoS) in BD-ΛCDM, weff, deviates from the standard -1 value of the ΛCDM model, exhibiting quintessence-like behavior for Δφ > 0. Numerical computations of weff at z = 0, taking into account the contributions from all terms, yield values that depart from -1, with the deviation reaching approximately 3σ confidence level when including the prior on H0 from the local distance ladder measurement and 3.5σ confidence level when also considering the angular diameter distances from H0LICOW. These results suggest that the BD-ΛCDM model can provide a better fit to observational data than the standard ΛCDM model, particularly in regards to the Hubble constant tension.

input: How does optimal transport solve for maximizing profits under treatment constraints?
expected_output: The optimal transport approach solves for maximizing profits under treatment constraints by mapping the distribution of conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) to a discrete distribution of assigned treatments. This is achieved through a two-step process, where the first step estimates the fully granular personalization solution, and the second step accounts for the constraint on the number of unique treatments available. The optimal transport problem in the second step aims to minimize the loss of profits from coarse personalization by choosing which treatments to offer and their assignments to get as close as possible to the fully granular profits. By forming segmenting and targeting decisions in concert, the firm is able to optimize to the correct metric, resulting in higher profits than those generated by first segmenting on covariates or preferences alone and then targeting. The optimal transport solution can be economically interpreted as choosing treatments and their assignments such that the average marginal benefit of treatment is equal to the marginal cost of treatment across assigned groups.
context:
Given the constraint that only {{formula:1c2a955a-70fb-4c67-a504-349a05eef9ff}} unique treatments can be offered,
the optimal transport problem in the second step solves for which
unique treatments to offer and who to assign to each treatment with
the goal of maximizing profits. In essence, the distribution of CATEs
that we estimated in the first step is mapped to a discrete distribution
of assigned treatments. We know that after the first step, the fully
granular personalization solution is profit maximizing for the firm
because it optimally chooses profit maximizing the treatment at the
individual level. The second step accounts for the extra constraint
and uses optimal transport to choose which treatments to offer and
their assignments to get as close as the fully granular profits as
possible. Our coarse personalization solution generates the maximum
expected profits possible given the limitation on the number of unique
treatments available to the firm.In terms of the traditional “STP” framework ,
we have solved both the segmentation and targeting steps in a single
procedure. The former are the assignments to each treatment and the
latter are the unique treatment values. Since we are discretizing
the fully granular personalization results into a handful of assigned
treatments in the second step, our “personalize then discretize”
approach inverts the “discretize then personalize” approach used
in classical “STP”. Because the optimal transport problem aims
to minimize profits lost from coarse personalization, its segmentation
and targeting results should yield higher profits than those generated
by first segmenting on covariates or preferences alone and then targeting.
By forming segmenting and targeting decisions in concert, the firm
is able to optimize to the correct metric. We further recover fully
granular profits when we let the number of treatments equal to the
number of individuals ({{formula:af1584cb-c02b-4c2c-8948-bb63907822de}} ). The final choice of the number of
unique treatments {{formula:6350f14e-b9b6-4833-995c-c183afb249e9}} to offer is left to the firm to tailor to its
setting.More generally, we espouse the optimal transport approach because
it allows us to interpret the coarse personalization problem in an
economic manner, suggests a simple procedure in Algorithm REF 
to solve it, and links it to a broader transport theory literature.
We can translate the optimization problem in Equation REF 
as a regret minimization problem – with a handful of treatments
available, the firm solves the problem to minimize lost potential
profits. Naturally, marketing researchers can use black-box optimizers
to solve the optimization program instead using our optimal transport
framework. However, in doing so, it loses the benefits from the optimal
transport approach. Section REF 's discussion
shows that we can economically interpret optimal transport solution
as choosing treatments and their assignments such that the average
marginal benefit of treatment is equal to the marginal cost of treatment
across assigned groups. Our adaptation of Lloyd's Algorithm in Algorithm
REF provides a computationally simple
yet scalable solution to solve the optimization problem and whose
link would not be made clear without viewing the problem from an optimal
transport lens. Because our algorithm takes in the optimal treatments
for each individual, it is especially efficient in higher dimensions
as it searches over treatments at are close to the individual optimal
values. Compared to a black-box optimizer approach, our algorithm
embeds a “warm start” in the optimization process. Lastly, recasting
our coarse personalization problem as an semi-discrete optimal transport
problem allows us to connect our marketing problem to transportation
theory and exploring other links may prove fruitful for future research.Outside of the our empirical application where we revisited the traditional
“STP” procedure for promotions management, we can also adapt our
coarse personalization procedure to a variety of different marketing
applications.

input: How can subjective probability assignments be used to understand and impact quantum reality?
expected_output: Subjective probability assignments can be used to understand and impact quantum reality by recognizing that probabilities are not objective numbers that exist in nature, but rather a tool for making rational decisions based on incomplete information. In the context of quantum mechanics, this means that different observers can assign different probabilities to the same event, and these assignments can change as new information becomes available. By embracing this subjective nature of probability, researchers can develop a more nuanced understanding of quantum phenomena, such as nonlocality and the role of observation in shaping reality. This perspective is supported by the work of Bayesian theorists, such as Ed Jaynes, who argue that probability theory is a logical tool for making inferences based on incomplete information, rather than a description of an objective reality. Additionally, the concept of subjective probability can be used to explore the idea of "no surprises, no reality," which suggests that our understanding of reality is shaped by our expectations and probabilities, rather than by an objective reality that exists independently of our observations.

In particular, probability has no a priori connection to the frequency of outcomes in a repeated
experiment. It matters not whether that repetition is real or,
instead, imaginary and virtual.Let me just try to drive this home with two of the simplest possible
examples.(1) Consider a coin for which you have no reason to believe that a
head will occur over a tail in a toss. Now imagine that you flip
that coin an infinite number of times, tabulating the number of heads
and tails. Do you really believe that a frequency of precisely 1/2
must occur in the infinite limit? Answer this question to
yourself very honestly. What is to bar you from getting a head as
the outcome in literally every single toss? What is there in the
coin to favor a random-looking sequence to a nonrandom one? Nothing.
To say something like, “Well the nonrandom-looking sequences have
probability zero” is just to beg the question. For one thing, you
have to invoke the concept of probability again to even say it. For
another, even if you allow yourself that, it still carries no force:
just take the set of nonrandom-looking sequences and add to it any
sequence that you would consider a valid random one (i.e., one that
you believe could be generated by a repeated coin toss). That set
still has probability-measure zero, but now you would have to say
that that means the random-looking sequence could not be generated by
your imaginary coin. The point: probability has no direct
connection to frequency.(2) Consider now the case where I toss a coin repeatedly for you. I
assure you strongly that the coin is weighted 80–20 heads vs. tails
or 20–80, but I steadfastly refuse to tell you which way it
goes. What probability would you ascribe to the outcome of a head
upon my first toss? Fifty-percent of course. The point is, my
probability ascription is not your probability ascription. As I toss
the coin ever more, if you are rational, your probability ascription
will very likely approach mine, but there are no absolute
assurances. The point: again probability has no direct connection
to frequency. But also, two perfectly rational people can make
different probability assignments to the same experiment without
being inconsistent with each other. There is nothing objective about

input: What is the significance of self-dual Yang-Mills theory in the context of supersymmetric Yang-Mills equations?
expected_output: Self-dual Yang-Mills theory is significant in the context of supersymmetric Yang-Mills equations because it provides a framework for understanding the integrability and solvability of these equations. The self-dual Yang-Mills equations are a set of equations that describe the behavior of gauge fields in a supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, and they have been shown to be integrable in certain cases. This means that the equations can be solved exactly, and the solutions can be expressed in terms of known functions. The self-dual Yang-Mills theory has been used to study the properties of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories, including their scattering amplitudes and their behavior at high energies. Additionally, the self-dual Yang-Mills theory has been related to other areas of physics, such as string theory and twistor theory, which has led to new insights and discoveries in these fields. For example, Witten's work on perturbative gauge theory as a string theory in twistor space has led to a deeper understanding of the relationship between gauge theory and string theory. Overall, the self-dual Yang-Mills theory is an important area of research in theoretical physics, and its significance lies in its ability to provide a framework for understanding the behavior of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories and their connections to other areas of physics.

This means that \overline{F} belongs to the class \mathcal{RV}_{-\alpha} for some \alpha > 0, indicating that the tail of the distribution decays at a certain rate as the value of the variable increases. The regular variation of Z can be characterized by the existence of a measurable function b, such that t \mathbb{P}(Z > b(t)x) converges to x^{-\alpha} for all x > 0, as t approaches infinity. This behavior is crucial in understanding and modeling heavy-tailed distributions, which are commonly observed in various fields, including finance, insurance, and network science.

input: What effect does dot product similarity have on the constancy of Neural Tangent Kernels?
expected_output: The dot product similarity measure has a significant effect on the constancy of Neural Tangent Kernels (NTKs). Specifically, when a network is trained using contrastive losses that utilize dot product similarity, the change in weights can become arbitrarily large, even for arbitrarily wide neural networks, implying that the NTK does not remain constant. This is because the loss can be minimized arbitrarily by scaling the weights, leading to unbounded growth in the weights over time. As a result, the NTK, which is a measure of the similarity between the outputs of a neural network for different inputs, also changes significantly, and its constancy is not guaranteed. In fact, it has been shown that there exist cases where the NTK does not remain constant, even for logarithmic training time and arbitrarily wide networks, when trained under dot product similarity-based loss.

input: How does FEWNet outperform classical methods in minimizing empirical risk for non-stationary, nonlinear BRIC CPI forecasting?
expected_output: FEWNet outperforms classical methods in minimizing empirical risk for non-stationary, nonlinear BRIC CPI forecasting by utilizing a combination of wavelet decomposition and autoregressive neural networks that incorporate exogenous variables. The wavelet decomposition stage allows for the filtering of the time series, yielding a hierarchical structure of new time series that facilitates their modeling and forecasting. This approach enables FEWNet to effectively capture the non-stationary and nonlinear patterns present in the BRIC CPI inflation series, resulting in more accurate predictions. Additionally, the use of autoregressive neural networks allows FEWNet to establish a functional relationship between the target series and the input vector, minimizing the predictive error and reducing the empirical risk. Overall, FEWNet's hybrid approach enables it to outperform classical methods in terms of minimizing empirical risk and providing more accurate forecasts for non-stationary, nonlinear time series.

In our study, we consider the monthly CPI numbers for BRIC countries from 2003-01 to 2021-11 released by FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis). These series are not adjusted for any seasonal patterns. The CPI series for all four countries are then converted to headline (HL) inflation numbers, described as Year-on-Year growth rate (persistent rise in the general price level) in the CPI series using the following approach:\pi _{\text{Jan }}^{2003}=\left[\frac{C P I_{J a n}^{2003}-C P I_{\text{Jan }}^{2002}}{C P I_{J a n}^{2002}}\right] * 100 \%,where \pi _{Jan }^{2003} denotes the derived CPI inflation number for 2003-Jan, calculated using CPI values of 2003-Jan and 2002-Jan (prior year and same month). In addition to the CPI inflation, we also consider the impact of two uncertainty measures, namely the EPU and GPRC index, on the future projections of CPI inflation numbers for the BRIC countries. As part of the data pre-processing step, we perform the log transformation on the EPU series to stabilize its variance. Sequentially, we decompose the CPI inflation, log-transformed EPU, and GPRC series using the Hodrick and Prescott (HP) filter and the Christiano-Fitzgerald (CF) random walk filter . These economic filters play a vital role in extracting the trends and business cycles associated with the time series. Further details on the HP filter and CF filter are provided in Appendix REF .In the analysis, we study the global features of the CPI inflation series, log-transformed EPU series, and GPRC series to identify their structural patterns and detect appropriate techniques for long-term forecasting. Primarily we focused on six popular time series characteristics, including skewness, kurtosis, non-linearity, long-range dependence, seasonality, and stationarity . To assess the long-range dependency of the time series, we utilize the Hurst exponent. To analyze the non-linear characteristics of the series, we employ Tsay's test and Keenan's one-degree test for non-linearity. To determine the stationarity of the series, we conduct the Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin test. Lastly, to identify any seasonal patterns in the series, we apply the Ollech and Webel's test.
The results of the statistical features, summarized in Table REF , depict that most of the macroeconomic time series are non-stationary except for the GPRC series of Brazil and the CPI inflation data of China. The majority of these series are positively skewed except for the log-transformed EPU series of Russia. Furthermore, most of the economic time series exhibit non-linear patterns which plays a crucial role in selecting the appropriate modeling approach for the dataset. Additionally, based on Ollech and Webel's seasonality test and the Hurst exponent we observe that all the series are non-seasonal and are characterized by long-range dependency. Moreover, the ACF and PACF plots of the CPI inflation series (presented in Table REF ) depict the presence of serial autocorrelation.

These inherent patterns of the CPI inflation series motivate the design and application of hybrid forecasting approaches for long-term forecasting.

expected_output:
The process for computing the energetic contribution using the Parisi PDE involves several steps. First, the Parisi PDE is given by the equation $\dot{f}(x,h) = - \frac{\dot{q}(x)}{2} \big [f^{\prime \prime }(x,h) + x f^{\prime }(x,h)^2\big ]$, where $x \in (0,1)$. The boundary condition for this equation is $f(1,h) = \log \gamma _{1-q(1)}(h)$. To compute the energetic contribution, we need to solve the Parisi PDE with the given boundary condition. 

In the case of the energetic contribution, the Parisi PDE is analytically solvable, and the solution can be found in the form $f(x,h) = \frac{1}{x} \log C(x) + \frac{1}{x} \log \gamma _{\omega (x)}(h)$. This yields simple ODEs on $\omega $ and $C$ that can be solved to obtain $\omega (x) = \frac{1 - x q(x) - \int _x^1 q(u) u}{x}$ and $\log C(x) = \frac{x}{2} \int _x^1 \frac{u}{u^2} [1 + \log 2\pi \omega (u)]$. 

Finally, the energetic contribution can be computed by taking the $r \rightarrow 0$ limit in the equation $- \frac{1}{2} \partial _r [\log \det ]_{r = 0} = \frac{\log 2\pi }{2} + \gamma _{q_m} \star f (0,h = 0)$, which yields the solution to the Parisi PDE for the entropic contribution.

input: What is the comparative performance of ESAC against Inspect, Pilliat, and other similar methods in terms of accuracy or efficiency?
expected_output: The comparative performance of ESAC against Inspect, Pilliat, and other similar methods, such as Sparsified Binary Segmentation and Double CUSUM, is evaluated in terms of accuracy and efficiency in the context of high-dimensional changepoint detection and estimation. The ESAC method is compared to these state-of-the-art methods through simulation studies, where the choice of penalty parameters is discussed for each method. The results show that ESAC performs competitively with these methods, with its performance being influenced by factors such as the magnitude of changes in the mean and the noise level in the data. In terms of efficiency, the running times of the methods are reported, with ESAC being implemented in the C programming language and run using R on a MacOS computer with an ARM Apple M1 Pro CPU. Overall, the comparative performance of ESAC against Inspect, Pilliat, and other similar methods demonstrates its potential as an effective and efficient method for high-dimensional changepoint detection and estimation.
context: In this section we compare the empirical performance of ESAC with the following state-of-the-art methods for high-dimensional changepoint detection and estimation: a variant of the Inspect method by , the method of hereby called Pilliat, Sparsified Binary Segmentation of , the Double CUSUM algorithm of , and the SUBSET method by . We introduce a slightly modified variant of Inspect, based on Narrowest-over-Threshold search, mainly to reduce computational cost. The details of our modified Inspect algorithm can be found in Appendix REF . To run the Sparsified Binary Segmentation and Double CUSUM algorithms, we use the R package hdbinseg . To run SUBSET, we use the code from the Github repository of . We have implemented the remaining methods ESAC, Pilliat and Inspect in the C programming language, and the implementations are found in the R package hdcd . Whenever running times are reported, they are run using R (4.2.1) on a MacOS (12.3) computer with an (ARM) Apple M1 Pro CPU.For each method in the simulation study, a choice of penalty parameters must be made, which is discussed in each section. In all simulations, changes in mean are taken to have magnitudes spread evenly across all affected coordinates. In Appendix REF we run the same simulations with uneven and random magnitudes, giving similar results. In all simulations we assume \sigma =1 is unknown. We estimate \sigma separately for each of the p coordinates of the observed time series, and use it to normalize the data before applying each changepoint detection method. As is commonly done in the changepoint literature, we estimate the noise level by the median absolute deviation of first-order differences with scaling factor 1.05 for the Gaussian distribution.

input: How do Tanaka and Levi-Tanaka algebras compare in CR geometry?
expected_output: In CR geometry, Tanaka and Levi-Tanaka algebras are closely related concepts that play a crucial role in understanding the geometric properties of CR structures. The Tanaka algebra, also known as the Tanaka prolongation, is a graded Lie algebra that is associated to a CR manifold and determines its geometric properties to a large extent. On the other hand, the Levi-Tanaka algebra is a specific type of Tanaka algebra that is associated to a Levi non-degenerate CR manifold. The Levi-Tanaka algebra is a fundamental invariant of the CR structure and encodes important information about the geometry of the manifold. In essence, the Tanaka algebra provides a general framework for studying CR geometry, while the Levi-Tanaka algebra is a more specialized concept that applies to a specific class of CR manifolds. Both algebras are used to study the equivalence problem of CR structures and have been extensively used in the study of CR geometry.

input: How can string theory's inflationary potential be used to explain the origin of the Universe's structure?
expected_output: String theory's inflationary potential can be used to explain the origin of the Universe's structure by providing a framework for understanding the evolution of the Universe during the inflationary era. In string theory, the inflationary potential is generated by the interactions of various fields, including the inflaton field, which drives the inflationary expansion. The potential depends on the specific string theory model and the configuration of the fields, and it can give rise to different types of inflation, such as single-field or hybrid inflation. By analyzing the properties of the inflationary potential, researchers can make predictions about the observational signatures of inflation, such as the spectral index of the density perturbation, which can be tested against observational data. Furthermore, string theory provides a framework for understanding the origin of the Universe's structure in terms of the fundamental interactions and fields that govern the behavior of the Universe at the level of field theory, which is hoped to be an approximation to some more fundamental theory like weakly coupled string theory or Horava-Witten M-theory. Ultimately, the goal is to find a string theory model that can accurately describe the observations and provide a consistent explanation for the origin of the Universe's structure.

In the face of increasingly accurate observations of
the cosmic microwave background anisotropy and of the galaxy

seems to provide the only known origin for structure in the Universe.
In this review we have seen how to build models of inflation, and test
them against observation.What is the point of such an exercise? To address this question, one
needs to understand what is meant by a model of inflation.
One can think of a model as something analogous to a building.
It has an outer shell, which is visible to the casual observer,
but hopefully also something inside.The shell is a specification of the form inflationary potential.
In a single-field model the potential
depends only on the inflaton field,
while in a hybrid model it depends on one or more additional fields.
Observation, notably through the spectral index of the density
perturbation, can discriminate sharply between different shells.
Most, and perhaps all, of the present zoo of shells will be
rejected by observations in the next ten to fifteen years,
culminating with the Planck satellite that will give an essentially
complete measurement of the cmb anisotropy.
One can imagine that
eventually just one basic form for the shell is singled out by the community,
which
by virtue of its intrinsic beauty and
its accurate description of the observations is likely to be the
one chosen by Nature.
Then, in a sense, there will be a consensus about
the origin of all structure in the Universe.

it probably comes from a certain scalar field potential!Things are very different when
we come to consider the interior of the
shell. Here, one recognizes that the inflationary potential is part
of an
the extension of the

fundamental interactions at the level of field theory. The field theory
description is, hopefully, an approximation to some more fundamental
theory like weakly coupled string theory or Horava-Witten M-theory.

not inevitable as we have seen in more than one example.At this point, inflation model-building becomes part of
the enterprise that has occupied the particle physics community
for more than two decades. That is, to find the extension of the
Standard Model that has been chosen by Nature.This is the usual viewpoint but one can vary it.
Maybe there is only one mathematically consistent theory that gives
anything resembling physical reality, in which case we have in principle
little need of observation. Maybe the usual assumption that there
are many possible theories is correct, but many or all of them
have been realized by Nature
in different parts of the universe, that may or may not be
connected with the homogeneous Universe around us. These variations make
no difference for the present purpose.

little guidance from observation, this enterprise has been driven by
theoretical considerations to an extent that is unprecedented in the
history of science. In particular, the rich structure of supersymmetry
is almost always assumed because it seems to be the only way of avoiding

input: What enables Ishikawa graphs to achieve optimal minima via max-flow, and how does edge capacity contribute to this outcome?
expected_output: Ishikawa graphs can achieve optimal minima via max-flow because they represent multi-label submodular energy functions with non-negative edge capacities. The non-negative edge capacities in Ishikawa graphs enable the optimal minimization of the energy function through max-flow, as the max-flow algorithm can effectively find the minimum cut in the graph, which corresponds to the optimal solution of the energy function. The edge capacities contribute to this outcome by defining the weights of the connections between nodes in the graph, allowing the max-flow algorithm to compute the optimal flow and thereby minimize the energy function.

submodular energy function can be represented by an Ishikawa graph with
non-negative edge capacities {{formula:5485856b-1a52-4a01-87e4-3dcf407a6068}} and can therefore be minimized optimally
by max-flow.

Since our algorithm can simply replace standard max-flow in Ishikawa-type
graphs, we replaced the BK method with our MEMF procedure in the IRGC
algorithm , which minimizes MRFs with some non-convex
pairwise potentials (or regularizers) by iteratively building and solving an
Ishikawa graph.
This lets us tackle much larger non-submodular problems. In particular, we
computed inpainting results on Penguin by using all 256 labels, as opposed to the down-sampled
label sets used in . The results of the IRGC+expansion
algorithm, with the BK method and with MEMF are
summarized in Table REF .

input: How do F4 and F5 quantify vertex connectivity in graph theory?
expected_output: F4, the local clustering coefficient (LCC), quantifies vertex connectivity by measuring the fraction of a vertex's neighbors that are also connected to each other, thereby capturing the small world phenomenon. F5, eigencentrality, quantifies vertex connectivity by representing the degree to which a vertex is connected to other vertices that are also highly connected, providing a measure of local "denseness" and indicating a higher probability of being part of a large clique.
context:
We use the following graph-theoretic features: (F1) number of vertices, (F2) number of edges, (F3) vertex degree, (F4) local clustering coefficient (LCC), and (F5) eigencentrality.The crude information captured by features (F1)-(F3) provide a reference for the classifier for generalizing to different distributions from which the graph might have been generated.
Feature (F4), the LCC of a vertex is the fraction of its neighbors with which the vertex forms a triangle, encapsulating the well-known small world phenomenon.
Feature (F5) eigencentrality represents a high degree of connectivity of a vertex to other vertices, which in turn have high degrees as well.
The eigenvector centrality {{formula:ecbe2308-3001-4af4-81ac-99889d3ddf94}} is the eigenvector of the adjacency matrix {{formula:aabc3092-e9bc-4c3d-b1d7-46d46672940e}} of {{formula:223212f2-cdfb-45db-b753-6cd111cea891}} with the largest eigenvalue {{formula:a59b2af1-17ea-4198-ba69-b3e8fe64be41}} , i.e., it is the solution of {{formula:49c23e9a-9124-4d29-ad44-3c310196e093}} .
The {{formula:5afba120-c121-4415-8821-981b621a8a3a}} th entry of {{formula:676f8bbc-689e-473f-9405-7f30637dcf5b}} is the eigencentrality of vertex {{formula:a8848c43-80ad-4a72-b637-9199072bb52b}} . In other words, this feature provides a measure of local “denseness”. A vertex in a dense region shows higher probability of being part of a large clique.

We experiment on structured datasets from diverse domains such as biological networks, financial graphs, social interaction and blog conversations.
Again, our instances are obtained from Network Repository .

Then, all the resulting tuples are collected in an array, which is sorted lexicographically in O(p log p) time, and duplicates are removed with another scan. The resulting array contains the set of intervals, sorted by the first coordinate, and is of size p'. Using this array, the array S is computed in O(p') time, and the set P is constructed in O(p') time. Finally, the structure from print-int-int-2 is constructed for P in O(p' log p') = O(p log p) time. Overall, the total time spent is O(p * (t_cmp log n + t_count + t_minocc)) + O(p log p), which simplifies to O(p * (t_cmp log n + t_count + t_minocc)) because the O(p log p) term is dominated by the other term for large p.

input: What are the advantages of the SI strategy over P and SD in terms of 3D object recognition accuracy?
expected_output: The surface-independent sampling (SI) strategy has advantages over the alternatives of sampling from the input points (P) and surface-dependent sampling (SD) in terms of 3D object recognition accuracy, as it outperforms the rest in quantitative comparisons. The network trained by the SI strategy achieves higher accuracy, and the per-point SOCS estimation error is as accurate in unseen regions as it is near the observed surface, demonstrating the necessity of surface-independent sampling and the efficacy of the feature propagation mechanism.

For ModelNet40-partial, we report the rotational error, and the translational error in the form of mean, and median values. We also report the average precision of instances for which the error is less than 5^{\circ } for rotation and 5cm for translation.

We have discussed the advantages of the surface-independent sampling (SI) strategy in Section . input: What are the primary challenges hindering unified progress in recommendation systems research?
expected_output: The primary challenges hindering unified progress in recommendation systems research are the lack of unified metrics to evaluate across papers, the absence of unified datasets to test on, and the limited availability of good features and complete raw input data in most datasets. Additionally, the field is hindered by the lack of a shared and well-maintained leaderboard on winning solutions, which makes it difficult to compare the performance of different algorithms. These challenges are further complicated by the use of different evaluation metrics, such as root mean square errors and ranking metrics, and the varying training-test splits used in different papers.
context:
In the process, motivated by the need to prevent over-fitting caused by the additional parameters, we introduced a general regularization technique for embedding layers in deep learning in chapter 6, which was shown to be useful for many other models with lots of embedding parameters both within and outside recommendations.

Future Work
Despite that the dissertation is lengthy and has contained many important research directions, it is by no means complete and I feel there are still many interesting and important directions worth pursuing but not done within this dissertation. I imagine at the end of day, assuming the computing power catches up, it is very likely we can discard most of the feature engineering and directly learn from raw data formats such as texts, images and videos, just like what happened in computer vision and natural language processing fields with the advances of deep learning techniques. This has not yet happened in neither academics or industry. To make this happen, I believe that there are a few shortcomings in current research practices:

There do not exist unified metrics to evaluate across papers. Some papers use root mean square errors (RMSE) as accuracy metric while others use ranking metrics. Then even within the ranking metrics, people tend to use different metrics: from AUC score to NDCG, precision and recall, not to mention that different top {{formula:4385dfa9-7f51-48a3-a718-77681b99bbbd}} can be used for NDCG, precision and recall.

There do not exist unified datasets to test on across papers. There are many datasets outside there, from Netflix to Movielens, and Douban to Flixster, etc.. Different papers tend to use different training-test splits: some do random splits while others do splits based on temporal orderings. Moreover, the recommender systems community does not really have a shared and well-maintained leader-board on the winning solutions. The results of various proposed algorithms are very likely to perform differently on different datasets.

Most datasets do not come with good features nor complete raw input data. To some extent, it is understandable because of the strict privacy and copyright concerns. But this has put academic researches at a disadvantage and often industry applied research will not take as much risk to pursue long-term projects. On the other hand, academics are able to take more risks to pursue longer-term research topics but unfortunately are limited by the constraints of good datasets and powerful computing resources.

While addressing these shortcomings, I think it would be very exciting to see different levels of interactions between the recommendation field and other AI fields, including natural language understanding and computer vision. News/Book recommendation, image recommendation, video recommendation and audio recommendation are some promising examples that may see breakthroughs of new models, just as what happened during Netflix competition about 10 years ago . But to do that, we need a well-defined problem, dataset and metric, and lots of people participating both from academics and industry by combining strengths from both parties.

input: What causes the variation in DLA and LLS formation in relation to the distances of LAE halos?
expected_output: The variation in DLA and LLS formation in relation to the distances of LAE halos is caused by the fact that not all Lyα emitting gas gives rise to optically thick absorbers, but only a fraction of the Lyα halos to distances of approximately 100 kpc appears to be covered by LLSs. According to Lofthouse et al., this fraction is estimated to be around 0.25, indicating that only a quarter of the Lyα halos within this distance range are associated with LLSs. Additionally, the formation of DLAs and LLSs is also influenced by the density of the gas, with higher densities leading to the formation of optically thick absorbers. The distance between LAE halos and LLSs, with LAEs often encountered at distances of greater than 100 kpc from LLSs, including in filamentary structures connecting galaxies, also plays a role in the variation of DLA and LLS formation.
context:
At face value, this result implies that LAE halos are responsible for the observed population of DLAs and LLSs in quasar surveys within radii of \approx 30 kpc and \gtrsim 60 kpc, respectively.
Further insight into this association can be gained by performing the opposite experiment, i.e., searching LAEs around the location of known LLSs. In the MUSE Analysis of Gas around Galaxies (MAGG), Lofthouse et al. find that LAEs are often encountered at distances of >100 kpc from LLSs, including in filamentary structures connecting galaxies. Lofthouse et al. estimate this fraction in the order of f_c\approx 0.25.

The ability to image the diffuse gas outside galaxies at even more considerable distances, reaching the IGM, would provide a complete view of how galaxies assemble within cosmic structures and how gas is exchanged between the cosmic web and the CGM, a critical component for comprehensive mapping the baryon cycle.
However, directly imaging the cosmic web is less trivial than the CGM, as the densities involved are even lower than for the CGM, reaching the mean cosmic density (\approx 10^{-5.5} cm^{-3} at z\approx 3). Moreover, the primary emission mechanisms are fluorescence from the UVB and cooling radiation. Additionally, the YN FSI can be accounted for by incorporating the final-state interaction between the hyperon (Y) and the nucleon (N) in the calculation. However, in the given context, the YN FSI is ignored, and the main lack of precision comes from this omission. A more accurate calculation would require the inclusion of the YN FSI, which could be achieved by using a more sophisticated model that takes into account the interaction between the hyperon and the nucleon.

input: What limitations arise from using variable IMF in galaxy evolution predictions?
expected_output: The use of variable Initial Mass Functions (IMFs) in galaxy evolution predictions gives rise to several limitations. One major limitation is the difficulty in disentangling the predictions of different models, particularly at smaller stellar masses where a larger fraction of stars are born from a reference IMF. Additionally, variable IMFs have a differential effect on the shape of the galaxy mass functions, which depends on both stellar mass and redshift, making it challenging to interpret galaxy evolution from observed photometry. Another limitation is that systematic IMF variations can lead to critical problems for algorithms trying to recover galaxy physical parameters from observed photometry, as these algorithms are often sensitive only to the dominant stellar component. This results in a substantial intrinsic scatter when comparing dynamically derived mass-to-light ratios to the predictions of stellar population models. Furthermore, the use of variable IMFs increases the number of fitted parameters and the level of degeneracies, potentially reducing the significance of the estimated physical quantities. As a result, it is not possible to include the statistical distribution of galaxy physical properties in the calibration sample for theoretical models under the hypothesis of a variable IMF. A more robust calibration would require a direct comparison with photometric properties of galaxy populations, such as multi-wavelength luminosity functions or number counts, which would involve evolving spectrophotometric codes to accommodate arbitrary shaped IMFs in the Semi-Analytic Model (SAM) framework.

In gravitational theory, energy conditions impose constraints on matter distributions, serving as essential guidelines for formulating a physically valid energy-momentum tensor. These conditions offer a framework for analysing the properties of matter distributions without requiring detailed knowledge of the internal composition. Consequently, phenomena such as the formation of geometric singularities or gravitational collapse during mergers can be studied without explicitly specifying the pressure or energy density. Fundamentally, the analysis of energy conditions is an algebraic problem , specifically an eigenvalue problem associated with the energy-momentum tensor. In a 4-dimensional space-time, evaluating these conditions involves solving a quartic polynomial to determine its eigenvalues, which can become analytically intricate. Despite the challenges in obtaining general solutions, a physically viable fluid distribution must satisfy the dominant, strong, weak, and null energy conditions, collectively referred to as the energy conditions, within the stellar configuration. input: How can BoW, LDA, and GOOD representations be utilized to optimize model-based object learning?
expected_output: The BoW, LDA, and GOOD representations can be utilized to optimize model-based object learning by carefully selecting and tuning their respective parameters to achieve a good balance between recognition performance, memory usage, and processing speed. For BoW and Local LDA, parameters such as dictionary size, image weighting, and spatial layout need to be optimized, while for LDA approaches, the number of topics also requires tuning. In the case of GOOD, the number of bins must be set optimally. By finding the optimal values for these parameters, the representations can be effectively used to improve the performance of the model-based object category learning approach.
context: The performance of the model-based object category learning approach was evaluated using BoW, LDA (standard and local) and GOOD representations. The variable-size representation approaches are not considered since most of the machine learning methods, including the proposed model-based learning approach, take fixed-length vectors as input. In the case of BoW and Local LDA, three parameters (IW, SL and DS) have different effects on both memory usage and recognition accuracy. Dictionary size (DS) determines the number of words in the dictionary. For LDA approaches, an additional parameter, NT is the number of topics. We tried to find a good value for these parameters to obtain a good balance between recognition performance, memory usage, and processing speed. In the case of GOOD, the number of bins, is the parameter that has to be set optimally. We describe in detail each set of experiments in the following subsections.

In this section, we develop an approach to autonomously construct models of unknown objects. This capability is necessary for cognitive robots, since it will allow robots to actively investigate their environments and learn about objects in an unsupervised and incremental way. Online construction of full surface models of objects is not only useful for improving object recognition performance by collecting several views, but also can be used for manipulation purposes.As shown in Fig. REF , our approach enables a robot to move around an object and build an increasingly complete 3D model of the object by extracting object's points from different perspectives and aligning them together by considering the tracked object pose and robot pose as well as geometrical and visual information. In such scenario, tracking the target object is necessary since many objects in everyday environments exhibit rotational symmetries or lack a distinctive geometry for matching. As stated by , without pose information, Iterative Closest Point (ICP) based approaches are unable to recover the proper transformations because of the ambiguity in surface matching. Towards this goal, we employ a Kalman filter that uses depth and visual information for keeping track of robot motion and the target object while it remains visible over time. Afterwards, the extracted object views are united using an incremental ICP http://pointclouds.org/documentation/tutorials/pairwise_incremental_registration.php#pairwise-incremental-registration approach  that incorporates both tracking and appearance information.It should be noted that this approach cannot provide information about regions of the target object that were not visible throughout the exploration procedure. Moreover, since the robot localization is out of the scope of this work, we use noisy ground truth information and showed that this approach can compensate the noise of robot motion and generate proper models of household objects. A video showing the robot exploring an environment for constructing a full model of an Amita juice box is available at: https://youtu.be/CuBS2L2q5NU

input: What causes long-range order in electronic systems via RG flow?
expected_output: The onset of long-range order in electronic systems is usually connected with a phase transition, and the renormalization group (RG) flow is a powerful tool for investigating these phase transitions. The RG flow is a process where the degrees of freedom are integrated out one after another, depending on their wavelength, and the change of the parameters from high to low energies is called the RG flow. In the context of electronic systems, the functional renormalization group (FRG) is used to study the flow of vertices, which are functions of the generalized quantum numbers of the degrees of freedom. The FRG has been employed to study instabilities of the Fermi surface of the 2D Hubbard model towards different symmetry-broken states, such as antiferromagnetism, superconductivity, and ferromagnetism. The flow equations for the vertices are derived using the definitions of the propagators and vertices, and the loop integrals are evaluated analytically or numerically. The RG flow causes long-range order in electronic systems by taking into account the modes that are integrated out through changes in the parameters of the action of the remaining modes, leading to a collective behavior of electrons that results in macroscopic effects.

Many of the phenomena in condensed matter physics can be understood as consequences of electronic correlations.
Superconductivity, magnetism, and the quantum Hall effects are just a few examples of how collective behavior of electrons leads to macroscopic effects. In many cases the main effects can be ascribed to some kind of longer-range order. It is thus an important task of condensed matter theory to shed light on the question why and how electrons order in different ways. If the order parameter is known or restricted to a few possibilities, much progress can been made within mean-field approaches like the BCS theory of superconductivity. On the other hand, the question if and how the electrons order in microscopic models such as the Hubbard model is still not resolved in general. One reason for this question still being open is that various ordering tendencies strongly influence and compete with each other.The onset of long-range order is usually connected with a phase transition. One of the most powerful tools for the investigation of phase transitions is the renormalization group (RG), laid out in its most common form by Wilson in 1971 . Wilson's RG is formulated in terms of the partition function of the system, that is, a functional integral over the degrees of freedom of the system.
The idea is to integrate out the degrees of freedom one after another depending on their wavelength, in contrast to perturbation theory, where all modes are treated simultaneously. One begins at high energies and short wavelengths and works one's way down to low energies, taking into account the modes that are integrated out through changes in the parameters of the action of the remaining modes. This process is called renormalization, and the change of the parameters from high to low energies is called the RG flow.Later, Polchinski formulated the renormalization group as an exact flow equation for the partition function of the theory. In the following, this was generalized to other generating functionals, such as the one for one-particle irreducible (1PI) vertices that will be used in this work. The flow equations for this generating functional were first derived for scalar fields by Wetterich , and later for fermionic systems, . By now it has been widely used to investigate many-fermion systems in various contexts (e.g. Refs. zanchi,halboth,rice,katanin,tempflow,wang.
In these systems the dominant question is which type of symmetry-breaking takes place at the transition, while the precise nature of the transition is often only of secondary interest.
For the RG schemes used in this context, the term functional renormalization group applies to the method in its present form in a twofold way: one uses a flow equation for a generating functional of fermionic fields to obtain flow equations for vertices, which are in turn functions of the generalized quantum numbers (wavevectors, Wannier orbitals) of the degrees of freedom. This has to be contrasted with usual RGs which are in general flow equations for just a small number of coupling constants.The functional RG was in particular employed to study instabilities of the Fermi surface of the 2D Hubbard model towards different symmetry broken states such as antiferromagnetism, superconductivity, and ferromagnetism by various researchers (e.g. Refs. zanchi,halboth,rice,katanin,tempflow). However, for technical reasons, it was not possible in these studies to obtain quantitative results for physical quantities like the order parameter, as the flows used were restricted to the symmetric phase. Instabilities in these studies would only show up in the form of diverging susceptibilities.

input: How do firms maximize profits via optimal transport for limited promotions?
expected_output: Firms can maximize profits via optimal transport for limited promotions by solving an optimal transport problem that determines which unique treatments to offer and who to assign to each treatment, with the goal of maximizing profits. This approach allows firms to form segmenting and targeting decisions in concert, optimizing to the correct metric, and yielding higher profits than traditional methods. By using optimal transport, firms can interpret the coarse personalization problem in an economic manner, minimize lost potential profits, and link it to a broader transport theory literature. The optimal transport approach also provides a simple procedure to solve the problem and allows for a "warm start" in the optimization process, making it especially efficient in higher dimensions. Additionally, firms can adapt this approach to various marketing applications, including promotions management, and use large-scale RCT data sets to estimate the optimal treatments for each individual.

Given the constraint that only {{formula:1c2a955a-70fb-4c67-a504-349a05eef9ff}} unique treatments can be offered,
the optimal transport problem in the second step solves for which
unique treatments to offer and who to assign to each treatment with
the goal of maximizing profits. In essence, the distribution of CATEs
that we estimated in the first step is mapped to a discrete distribution
of assigned treatments. We know that after the first step, the fully
granular personalization solution is profit maximizing for the firm
because it optimally chooses profit maximizing the treatment at the
individual level. The second step accounts for the extra constraint
and uses optimal transport to choose which treatments to offer and
their assignments to get as close as the fully granular profits as
possible. Our coarse personalization solution generates the maximum
expected profits possible given the limitation on the number of unique
treatments available to the firm.In terms of the traditional “STP” framework ,
we have solved both the segmentation and targeting steps in a single
procedure. The former are the assignments to each treatment and the
latter are the unique treatment values. Since we are discretizing
the fully granular personalization results into a handful of assigned
treatments in the second step, our “personalize then discretize”
approach inverts the “discretize then personalize” approach used
in classical “STP”. Because the optimal transport problem aims
to minimize profits lost from coarse personalization, its segmentation
and targeting results should yield higher profits than those generated
by first segmenting on covariates or preferences alone and then targeting.
By forming segmenting and targeting decisions in concert, the firm
is able to optimize to the correct metric. We further recover fully
granular profits when we let the number of treatments equal to the
number of individuals ({{formula:af1584cb-c02b-4c2c-8948-bb63907822de}} ). The final choice of the number of
unique treatments {{formula:6350f14e-b9b6-4833-995c-c183afb249e9}} to offer is left to the firm to tailor to its
setting.More generally, we espouse the optimal transport approach because
it allows us to interpret the coarse personalization problem in an
economic manner, suggests a simple procedure in Algorithm REF 
to solve it, and links it to a broader transport theory literature.
We can translate the optimization problem in Equation REF 
as a regret minimization problem – with a handful of treatments
available, the firm solves the problem to minimize lost potential
profits. Naturally, marketing researchers can use black-box optimizers
to solve the optimization program instead using our optimal transport
framework. However, in doing so, it loses the benefits from the optimal
transport approach. Section REF 's discussion
shows that we can economically interpret optimal transport solution
as choosing treatments and their assignments such that the average
marginal benefit of treatment is equal to the marginal cost of treatment
across assigned groups. Our adaptation of Lloyd's Algorithm in Algorithm
REF provides a computationally simple
yet scalable solution to solve the optimization problem and whose
link would not be made clear without viewing the problem from an optimal
transport lens. Because our algorithm takes in the optimal treatments
for each individual, it is especially efficient in higher dimensions
as it searches over treatments at are close to the individual optimal
values. Compared to a black-box optimizer approach, our algorithm
embeds a “warm start” in the optimization process. Lastly, recasting
our coarse personalization problem as an semi-discrete optimal transport
problem allows us to connect our marketing problem to transportation
theory and exploring other links may prove fruitful for future research.Outside of the our empirical application where we revisited the traditional
“STP” procedure for promotions management, we can also adapt our
coarse personalization procedure to a variety of different marketing
applications.

This property is distinct from other methods in that it provides a canonical extension, meaning that the extended map Ĥ is uniquely determined by the original map F. In the context of extending linear maps to End(W), this means that any linear map F: V → End(W) can be extended to a unique algebra homomorphism Ĥ: T(V) → End(W), which can be used to simplify the nth Picard iterate. This is in contrast to other methods, which may not provide a unique or canonical extension. Additionally, the universal property of T(V) allows for the extension of linear maps in a way that preserves the algebraic structure of the original map, which is not necessarily the case with other methods.

The following result, known as Prohorov's Theorem, describes a sufficient condition for a subset of probability measure to be relatively compact in the the topology of weak convergence. When the underlying space X is a Polish space, then this condition is also necessary.Theorem 4.25 (Prohorov's Theorem) 
Suppose X is a Lusin space. Then a subset H of \mathcal {P}(X) is relatively compact in the topology of weak convergence if H is tight in the sense that for any \epsilon >0 there exists compact subset K of X such that \mu (K^{c})<\epsilon for all \mu in H.From the point of view of these results, it would desirable for the property of Polishness to hold in the case X=\mathcal {C}_{p}. This fails however for the product topology as the following result shows. In fact we show more, namely that for p=1 the topological space (\mathcal {C}_{1},\tau _{\text{pr}}) is not a Baire space. We recall this means that any countable union of closed sets with empty interior itself has empty interior. Any (pseudo-)metrisable space is a Baire space, and in particular any Polish space is a Baire space. The proof we give here relies on the Lyons-Xu construction discussed in Example REF , which the reader may wish to re-read before diving into the details.Theorem 4.26 
The topological space (\mathcal {C}_{1},\tau _{\text{pr}}) is not a Baire space and so not completely metrisable. In particular, it is not a Polish space.Proposition REF gives us that \mathcal {C}_1 = \bigcup _{r=1}^{\infty }B(r) where B(r) is the compact subspace of \chi _{\text{pr}}. As (\mathcal {C}_{1},\tau _{\text{pr}}) is a Hausdorff space, these sets must also be closed. By definition, each element of B(r) has tree-reduced length bounded by r, and, by Proposition REF , B(r) cannot therefore contain any non-trivial open subset. It follows that \mathcal {C}_1 is the countable union of closed sets each having empty interior and thus is not a Baire space.One might ask whether by selecting a different induced topology more desirable properties could be arrived at. input: How can Loop Quantum Cosmology's holonomy and triad variables be used to analyze the collapse of a dust cloud?

The first quantization, based on standard Loop Quantum Cosmology, utilizes holonomy and triad variables to derive an effective Hamiltonian and equations of motion, allowing for analytical solutions in certain cases. In addition to the effective Hamiltonian and the equations of motion in each case, we also discuss analytical solutions in the first case and define useful variables for unravelling the dynamics of the collapsing dust cloud through numerical results when analytical solutions are not available.

input: What are the limitations of using Hoeffding-type inequalities with missing data in terms of exponential decay?
expected_output: The limitations of using Hoeffding-type inequalities with missing data in terms of exponential decay are that they are currently missing in the literature, making it difficult to induce an exponentially decaying term in n. Specifically, the term P(T_n^* > xb_{m,n}(x)) is expected to have some form of exponential decay in x, but without comparable Hoeffding-type inequalities for the self-normalized sum, the desired exponential rate of decay in n cannot be achieved. This gap in the literature is an important problem that deserves independent investigation to develop such inequalities.

input: How does the SGT method compare to the Bonferroni method in controlling type-1 errors?
expected_output: The SGT method is compared to the Bonferroni correction in controlling type-1 errors, with the SGT method aiming to maximize power by using a carefully designed multiple testing approach that prioritizes a smaller set of promising hypotheses, thereby avoiding the severe multiplicity correction inherent in the Bonferroni method. The SGT method uses a graph-based approach to allocate the error budget, allowing for more efficient control of type-1 errors, whereas the Bonferroni method applies a uniform correction across all hypotheses, which can be overly conservative. By using SGT with a fallback procedure or a Hamming graph, the method can tightly control non-monotonic risks and provide more precise control over type-1 errors compared to the Bonferroni method.
context:
This fact is even more surprising given our use of various advanced techniques in uniform concentration that yield sharp constants , .
Roughly, the reason for this conservativeness is that the existing techniques to derive the concentration inequalities apply the union bound (i.e., the Bonferroni correction) over a large grid of values.
By contrast, a carefully designed multiple testing approach judiciously prioritizes a smaller set of promising hypotheses, avoiding the severe multiplicity correction.Turning to open questions, we first mention what has become a standard surgeon-general's warning in the field of distribution-free statistics: all of the guarantees in this paper are marginal.
The reader should internalize what this means: we cannot guarantee that the errors are balanced over different strata of {{formula:5f7ded4d-091d-45e8-8e0a-89cd85736d84}} - and {{formula:4841be3a-2031-4fdd-9369-5b6f637e87c6}} -space, even meaningful ones such as object class, race, sex, illumination, et cetera.
All of the errors may occur in one pathological bin—although it is possible to guard against such behaviors by designing a good score and evaluating the algorithms over relevant strata . Extending the proposed techniques to have errors exactly or approximately balanced across strata is an open direction of great importance.The work presented herein opens many other questions for future work.
We have not explored the question of optimal testing procedures—neither when they exist, nor what they would be, nor when they are SGTs.
Additionally, the SGTs used above are relatively simple and somewhat hand-designed heuristic procedures.
One could hope to do better by learning the graph from another data split.
We are not aware of work addressing this topic—such methods would not have been relevant in the medical statistics community that originated SGTs.
On a different note, the capability to tightly control non-monotonic risks should enable computer scientists and statisticians in many applied areas to more carefully audit and certify their algorithmic predictions.
We hope our examples demonstrate to this community that, even in complex setups with sophisticated algorithms, pragmatic and explicit statistical guarantees are possible.
