input: How can mass-to-light ratios and galaxy colors be used to inform and improve stellar mass calculations?
expected_output: The mass-to-light ratio model, in conjunction with galaxy colors from SDSS ugriz and 2MASS JHK magnitudes, can be used to determine stellar masses. By utilizing the mass-to-light ratio model and incorporating galaxy colors, researchers can improve the accuracy of stellar mass calculations, as this approach allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the galaxy's composition and properties. This method has been employed in the context of the CLoGS sample, where stellar masses were determined using this approach, resulting in a range of stellar masses spanning a factor of approximately 5, from 4 × 10^10 to 26 × 10^10 M⊙.
context: To investigate the various properties and nature of the optical line-emitting gas in nearby BGGs, we observed with MUSE 18 sources drawn from the 26-member CLoGS high-richness sub-sample (RRichness (R) is defined as the number of galaxies within the group with B-band luminosity log L{{formula:0326aeb9-e3d9-4014-8ab9-5d53827d2290}} {{formula:68d49cfc-3f86-4bc5-9d60-07fbe54a3060}} 10.2 .{{formula:28eddcf7-946b-47c7-89a8-909df11b2739}} 4-8), . The CLoGS sample consists of 53 galaxy groups selected via friends-of-friends and hierarchical clustering algorithms from the LEDA (Lyon-Meudon Extragalactic Database; ) galaxy catalog . Worth noting that the groups were chosen to own an elliptical as a group-dominant galaxy. The CLoGS provides an ideal sample in which to study the origin of the gas within lower-mass systems. For the interested reader, a detailed description of the CLoGS sample selection criteria can be found in . In terms of stellar velocity dispersion (a proxy for gravitational potential), the MUSE sources show no significant difference from the other CLoGS group dominant galaxies in the high or low-richness sub-samples. Table REF and Table REF , summarize the MUSE observations and the main properties for each target, respectively.Our MUSE sample spans a wide range of stellar masses, SFRs, X-ray and radio properties. The stellar masses span a factor of approximately 5, from 4{{formula:37895394-2148-4fb0-91cb-16097610be47}} 10{{formula:86381937-2539-4d12-bb46-2d272b93eaa2}} to 26{{formula:cb655aec-aaa5-4f25-a26a-8afcee62cf9a}} 10{{formula:a0fabe4d-aa67-49b3-b846-75215d3d13ad}}  M{{formula:8be2987f-31e3-473f-a757-de8c7390f751}} , With NGC 1060 being the most luminous, and NGC 584 the dimmest. For comparison, BCGs have typical stellar masses higher than {{formula:42c6a63e-f26e-40c4-8c90-8a32ccc4e676}} 10{{formula:f0fbe277-14ba-4e6c-8745-dce0b1181a8e}}  M{{formula:341bb88b-826a-4c1a-9cf1-7d9981e7dc26}} . The stellar masses were determined using a mass-to-light ratio model, and using galaxy colors from SDSS ugriz and 2MASS (2 Micron All Sky Survey) JHK magnitudes .Optical emission line narrow-band spectroscopy had already been carried out for a couple of sources (NGC 584, NGC 5846, NGC 7619), by using narrow-band filter centered on the H{{formula:01913ea6-4e77-4c26-b0c3-5ea1b260c16a}} +[NII] emission lines from New Technology Telescope (NTT) . The authors identify different morphologies from compact up to filamentary as we also found in galaxy clusters.

As supported by high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations (see , for a review), we propose a possible evolutionary sequence for the multiphase gas: the filaments first condense out of the hot gas via CCA, followed by a transitional episode, where the gaseous threads will start to accrete onto the center to form a massive extended kiloparsec rotating star-forming disk in the galaxy. The raw material of the disk can then be consumed either by star formation activity (which can also provide feedback) or by fueling the center of the AGN, leading to a compact and quiescent rotating disk.This work was supported by the ANR grant LYRICS (ANR-16-CE31-0011). Additionally, the Smith form requires the computation of the integral matrix representation of the group, which can be computationally intensive for large groups. Furthermore, the Smith form only provides a normal form for the matrix representation, but does not necessarily provide a clear understanding of the underlying group structure or its properties.

input: Does the compTT model accurately capture the characteristics of Seyfert 1 soft excess, and can it be relied upon for precise astronomical predictions?
expected_output: The compTT model is found to successfully represent the soft excess in the Seyfert 1 galaxy, with a statistically acceptable fit of 902.6/923, corresponding to an F-test probability of 99.99%. The best-fit electron temperature of the Comptonization corona is consistent with previous results from the Seyfert 1 galaxy MCG 6-30-15. However, the optical depth is smaller, and there is a degeneracy between the temperature and optical depth that needs to be considered. The observed flux of this component is also consistent with expectations. While the compTT model accurately captures the characteristics of the Seyfert 1 soft excess, its reliability for precise astronomical predictions depends on further verification and consideration of the model's limitations and uncertainties.

input: What causes the differences in RT, ED, and EOG as the number of samples approaches infinity?
expected_output: The differences in RT, ED, and EOG as the number of samples approaches infinity are caused by the distinct coefficients and terms in their respective expansions. Specifically, the leading terms of these expansions, as found by McKay, have different coefficients and powers of n, which affect their behavior as n approaches infinity. For example, RT(n) has a leading term of n^{1/2} * (2^{n+1}/πn)(n-1)/2, while ED(n) has a leading term of n^{1/2} * (4^{n}/πn)(n-1)/2, and EOG(n) has a leading term of n^{1/2} * (3^{n+1}/4πn)(n-1)/2. These differences in coefficients and powers of n result in distinct asymptotic behaviors for RT, ED, and EOG as n approaches infinity.

input: What is the significance of Df in relation to the root repetition of f, and how does it impact the overall outcome?
expected_output: The significance of Df, the formal derivative of a polynomial f, lies in its relation to the repetition of roots of f. According to Lemma 2.9, a polynomial f has a repeated root in its splitting field if and only if f and Df have a common root in the splitting field, or equivalently, if and only if f and Df have a nonconstant common factor in K[t]. This means that the formal derivative Df can be used to test whether a polynomial has repeated roots. If Df shares a root with f, then f has a repeated root, indicating that the polynomial is not separable. This has significant implications for the properties of the polynomial and its splitting field, particularly in the context of Galois theory and the study of field extensions. The use of Df in this context provides an algebraic analogue to the real analysis test for repeated roots, which relies on the derivative of a function.

input: How can replicator equations be used to model infinite population dynamics?
expected_output: The replicator equations can be used to model infinite population dynamics by describing the evolutionary dynamics of interacting individuals in a deterministic manner. These equations are ordinary differential equations that track the fraction of individuals of each type in the population over time, with the assumption that individuals interact in a symmetric two-player normal form game specified by a payoff matrix. The average payoff per game to an individual of each type is calculated, and the replicator equations then describe how the composition of the population changes over time based on these payoffs. Specifically, the standard replicator equations are given by the equation \dot{x}_i = x_i(\pi _i - \pi ), where x_i is the fraction of individuals of type i, \pi _i is the average payoff to an individual of type i, and \pi is the average payoff across the entire population. These dynamics can be derived from a birth-death process in the limit of an infinite population, providing a framework for understanding how populations evolve over time in the absence of stochastic effects.

In this type of game one idea is dominant, and always has a higher payoff than the other type of idea. The replicator flow has constant sign; for the choice of payoff matrix in Fig. REF (b) it has an unstable fixed point at x=0, and a stable fixed point at x=1. The Sato-Crutchfield dynamics at \lambda >0 has an additional stable interior fixed point x^\star , which approaches unity as \lambda \rightarrow 0, see Fig. REF (a). In finite populations the dynamics is similar to that of the coexistence game when \lambda > 0. After an initial relaxation towards the interior fixed point, noise drives the system to fixation. Given that the fixed point is located close to x=1 for small and moderate \lambda , fixation will mostly occur at the upper absorbing boundary. As before fixation times increase with \lambda but are rather shorter than in the coexistence game, see Fig. REF (b). Exponential dependence of the fixation time on \lambda is only seen when \lambda is sufficiently large so that the internal fixed point is well separated from the absorbing states, or when the population size is large enough for the activation barrier to show. For small and moderate values of \lambda the activation barrier is too shallow relative to the noise strength for Eyring-Kramers theory to apply.

In the inset of panel (b) we show the mean fixation time starting from n = 1000 for a population of size 2000, where the crossover to an exponential dependence on \lambda is visible at large \lambda .]

The evolutionary dynamics of interacting individuals in infinite populations is frequently described by replicator or replicator-mutator equations. These are deterministic ordinary differential equations. We focus on a population of individuals of S different types, i=1,\dots ,S, and write x_i(t) for the fraction of individuals of type i in the population at time t, and \mathbf {x}=(x_1,\dots ,x_S). At all times \sum _i x_i(t)=1. We assume that individuals interact in a symmetric two-player normal form game hofbauer. This is specified by a payoff matrix \mathbf {A}=(a_{ij}). The entry a_{ij} is the payoff to an individual of type i in an interaction with an individual of type j. The setup of a symmetric game is not to be confused with a game for which the payoff matrix is symmetric, i.e. its own transpose.The average payoff per game to an individual of type i in a population of composition \mathbf {x} is given by \pi _i(\mathbf {x})=\sum _j a_{ij}x_j. In order to keep the notation compact, we will omit the argument \mathbf {x} in the following. The standard replicator equations are then given by hofbauer\dot{x}_i = x_i(\pi _i - \pi ),with \pi = \sum _j x_j \pi _j. These dynamics can be derived from a birth-death process in the limit of an infinite population. This will be discussed in more detail below.

input: What causes increased load buffer full stalls in pseudo-distributed big data analytics?
expected_output: The increased load buffer full stalls in pseudo-distributed big data analytics are caused by the participation of the full software stack, which increases memory access latency. This is because long latency memory accesses put pressure on the load buffer, as many load operations are in-flight and new load operations cannot be issued due to a lack of load buffer entries, resulting in a pipeline load buffer full stall. Additionally, the software stack's impact on L2 cache and data TLB behaviors also contributes to the increased load buffer full stalls, as L2 cache misses and data TLB misses can trigger long latency memory accesses. Overall, the combination of increased memory access latency and the software stack's effects on cache and TLB behaviors leads to increased load buffer full stalls in pseudo-distributed big data analytics.
context:
Load buffer is another very important unit along data path, and it also has great impact on CPI performance for big data analytics workloads as discussed in Section .
Each load micro-operation requires a load buffer entry and will access the data TLB and data cache.
The load buffer keeps track of in-flight loads in the out of order processor.
The load buffer full stall event records the cycles of stall due to lack of load buffer entry.
We calculate the ratio of load buffer full stall cycles to the total cycles the application used.
We also give the normalized value in Figure REF by using the standalone mode workloads as baseline.
From Figure REF , we can find that most of the applications running at pseudo-distributed mode have more load buffer full stalls than their standalone counterpart. The only exceptions are WordCount and PageRank, which seem not sensitive to software stack from the perspective of load buffer full stall.
The notable one is Sort, which has about 72.5 times more load buffer full stalls when the full software stack involved.Long latency memory accesses increase the load buffer's pressure since lots of load operations are in-flight and the new load operations can not be issued for lacking of load buffer entries, where a pipeline load buffer full stall occurs.
This phenomenon implies that the participation of full software stack increases memory access latency for most of big data analytics applications We also observe a similar phenomenon for store buffer. The applications run at pseudo-distributed mode have more store buffer full stalls than their standalone counterpart. However, the ratio is not as big as load buffer full stalls. The maximum ratio is about 1.6. For the store buffer full stall does not have a strong correlation with performance, we do not discuss it here..In Section  we find that the private united cache and TLB miss ratio have strong positive correlations with CPI. Also the private united cache (L2 cache) and TLB are key units along the data path.
Figure REF and Figure REF show the L2 cache MPKI (misses per thousand instructions) and data TLB MPKI. Here we also show the normalized value using standalone mode as baseline just as previous subsection does.We can find from Figure REF that for different applications the software stack has different impacts on L2 cache and data TLB behaviors.
For some applications, the pseudo-distributed mode has more L2 cache misses.
Such as K-means and Pagerank have 1.64 and 1.53 times as many L2 cache misses running on pseudo-distributed mode as running on standalone mode respectively.
Other applications have less cache misses after invoking the full software stack.
For example, psesudo-distributed mode Sort only has 20% L2 cache misses of its standalone counterpart.
For data TLB performance, we can find from Figure REF that nearly all of the big data analytics applications have more data TLB misses per thousand instructions when they run under the pseudo-distributed mode.
The notable one is K-means, which has 1.6 times more data TLB misses running at pseudo-distributed mode than running at standalone mode.
The only two exception are Sort, which has less data TLB misses when using full software stack (only 0.41 time of that of its standalone counterpart), and Fuzzy K-means, which seams insensitive to software stack from the perspective of data TLB behavior.
So for most of big data analytics applications, the participation of full software stack increases the burden of the data TLB.The L2 cache miss and data TLB miss can trigger long latency memory access. And we can find that some applications have less L2 cache and less data TLB MPKI whereas own more load buffer full stalls, such as Sort. Those phenomena are not inconsistent.

the context of digitalized information explosion,
more and more
businesses are analyzing massive amount of data – so-called big data –
with the goal of converting big data to “big value” by means of modern data center systems.
Typically, data center workloads can be classified into two categories: services and data analytics workloads as mentioned in and .
For the data analytics workloads always process a large mount of data in data centers, we call them big data analytics workloads. Typical big data analytics workloads include business intelligence, machine learning, bio-informatics, and ad hoc analysis , .The business potential of the big

innovative data center systems including both hardware and software, .
For example, the recommendation system is a typical example with

This paper seeks to address the above questions by characterizing representative big data analytics applications.

input: What is the process for developing a quantum GAN that mimics the architecture of classical GANs, and how can it be achieved?
expected_output: The process for developing a quantum Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that mimics the architecture of classical GANs involves several steps. First, a quantum discriminator is built, which is followed by the development of a quantum version of the generator. Then, the quantum equivalent of the zero-sum game is created, defining an objective loss function that acts on quantum states. This process allows for the creation of a quantum GAN that can learn to generate quantum states that are indistinguishable from real quantum data. The development of a quantum GAN involves the use of quantum circuits and quantum gates, such as controlled gates and activation functions, to implement the quantum discriminator and generator. By mimicking the classical GAN architecture, the quantum GAN can be trained to produce high-quality quantum states that can be used for various applications. Overall, the development of a quantum GAN requires a deep understanding of both quantum mechanics and machine learning principles.

input: What causes shared jumps to reduce variance in mixed partial derivative estimates?
expected_output: Shared jumps reduce variance in mixed partial derivative estimates because they lower the variance of the difference to a smaller value, rather than the larger value that would result from using only two processes. This occurs because the shared jumps synchronize the processes, allowing for a more accurate estimation of the mixed partial derivative. As a result, the variance of the difference is reduced to a value of 5×10^6, which is significantly smaller than the variance that would be obtained without shared jumps. This reduction in variance is a key benefit of using shared jumps in the estimation of mixed partial derivatives, and it is particularly important for achieving accurate results in computations involving complex models, such as the mRNA transcription model.

input: How does bootstrap variance estimation compare to IC-based TMLE variance estimation in terms of accuracy and reliability?
expected_output: The bootstrap variance estimation and the IC-based TMLE variance estimation differ in their approach to estimating the variance of the Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimator (TMLE). The IC-based TMLE variance estimation adjusts for the network-based dependence among units by using the estimated variance of the influence curves, whereas the bootstrap variance estimation uses a parametric bootstrap approach to estimate the TMLE variance. In terms of accuracy and reliability, the bootstrap variance estimation can achieve better performance, particularly in small samples, as it can provide better nominal coverage compared to the IC-based variance estimate. However, the IC-based variance estimation is also a valid approach that takes into account the network-based dependence among units, and its corresponding confidence intervals can be obtained from the "IC.CIs" list item. Overall, the choice between the two approaches depends on the specific context and the characteristics of the data, with the bootstrap variance estimation being a viable alternative to the IC-based variance estimation, especially in situations where small sample sizes are a concern.

input: What are the advantages of LXR's reference counting in optimizing dead object identification?
expected_output: LXR's reference counting with deferral, coalescing, and implicitly dead optimizations provides several advantages in optimizing dead object identification. The use of reference counting allows LXR to promptly identify dead objects, and the additional optimizations enable efficient collection of dead cycles and dead objects with stuck reference counts. Furthermore, LXR's approach results in substantially fewer RC pauses, retired instructions, and cache misses compared to other garbage collectors like G1 and Shenandoah, particularly on benchmarks such as avrora, sunflow, and xalan. This highlights the efficiency of LXR's targeted evacuation and increment processing during regular, brief stop-the-world pauses.
context:
LXR promptly identifies dead objects using reference counting with deferral , coalescing , and implicitly dead   optimizations, with a back-up concurrent trace  to collect dead cycles and dead objects with stuck reference counts.LXR uses regular, brief stop-the-world (STW) pauses to coherently scan runtime roots including mutator threads and stacks.
Compared to taking a more aggressive on-the-fly approach to almost entirely remove pauses ,
LXR instead uses STW pauses as opportunity for highly efficient, targeted evacuation (sec:alg-reclamation) and increment processing.

On the benchmarks where LXR performs the best (avrora, sunflow, and xalan), LXR has substantially fewer RC pauses, retired instructions, and cache misses (measured but unshown) than G1 and Shenandoah. LXR's improvements over Shenandoah highlight the CPU and memory penalties of region-based concurrent copying.

input: What impact do configuration files have on the topology and reinforcement learning behavior of NetSecGame?
expected_output: The configuration files have a significant impact on the topology and reinforcement learning behavior of NetSecGame. The first configuration file defines the network topology, including clients, servers, services, and data, which determines the scenario or environment in which the game is played. The second configuration file, stored with each agent, defines the behavior of the reinforcement learning part of the environment, including the presence of a defender agent, the specific scenario used, the maximum number of actions allowed, and the probability of success and detection for each action. These configuration files allow for flexibility and customization of the game environment, enabling the creation of different scenarios and the evaluation of various agents and strategies. The configuration files ultimately influence the performance of the agents, as evidenced by the win rates, average returns, and detection rates presented in the results, which vary depending on the scenario and configuration settings.
context:
NetSecGame uses two configuration files. The first is for defining the network topology, and the second is for defining the behavior of the RL part of the environment.The network topology configuration uses a configuration file from the CYST simulation environment . CYST was used since it is a flexible simulation engine based on network events. Different configuration files for the topology define different 'scenarios' as described in Subsection REF .The network topology configuration file defines:Clients: A client is defined as a Node with an IP address on an interface and the networks to which it is connected.

Servers: A server is defined as a Node with an IP address, a group of services, and the networks to which it is connected. The two routers in the environment (main router and Internet router) are servers with two interfaces.

Services: A service is defined with a description and what data is present on it.

Data: Data are strings stored in a service.The second configuration regarding the RL part of the environment is stored together with the configuration of each agent. It includes if there is going to be a defender agent or not, the specific scenario used, the maximum amount of actions allowed (steps), and for each action, the probability of success and the probability of detection (this last one only if there is a defender agent). An example configuration file can be found in the anonymized repository https://github.com/stratosphereips/NetSecGame/blob/main/agents/q_learning/netsecenv-task.yaml.

The win rates of all the agents in the small scenario with and without a defender are presented in Figure REF . The figures show the results in different max_steps settings. In the scenario without a defender, the ReAct agent wins 100% of the time in the 60 and 100 max_steps setting and outperforms the baselines clearly. When the max steps are limited to 30, it wins 80% of the time, which is still the best performance. The random agent with the no-repeat heuristic shows that, given enough steps, it eventually wins.
[Table: For the NetSecGame small scenario, average win rates, returns, and detection rates of all agents with random target per episode. With a maximum of 60 max_steps per episode and 30 episodes of repetition in LLM-based agents.]In addition to the win rates, Table REF shows the average returns and detection rates on the small scenario with 60 max_steps. The average returns show a similar view as the win rates. Regarding detection rates, the lowest detection rate is reported by the random agent (15.81%), with the ReAct agent closely following at 16.67%

&= \sum _{a \in S_t} (1-) w_t(a) + \sum _{a \notin S_t} w_t(a)\\
&= W_t - \sum _{a \in S_t} w_t(a).

Since we are using weighted majority vote, the incorrect prediction must have the majority vote:

\sum _{a \in S_t} w_t(a) \ge \tfrac{1}{2} W_t.

Therefore, if the algorithm makes mistake at round t, we have

W_{t+1} \le (1 - \tfrac{}{2}) W_t.

Combining with (REF ) and (REF ), we get

\frac{(1-)^{\mathtt {cost} ^*}}{K} < \frac{W_{T+1}}{W_1} = \prod _{t=1}^{T} \frac{W_{t+1}}{W_t} \le (1 - \tfrac{}{2})^M,

where M is the number of mistakes. Taking logarithm of both sides, we get

\mathtt {cost} ^* \cdot \ln (1-) - \ln {K} < M \cdot \ln (1-\tfrac{}{2}) < M \cdot (-\tfrac{}{2}),

where the last inequality follows from Fact . Rearranging the terms, we get

M < \mathtt {cost} ^* \cdot \tfrac{2}{} \ln (\tfrac{1}{1-}) + \tfrac{2}{} \ln {K}
< \tfrac{2}{1 - } \cdot \mathtt {cost} ^* + \tfrac{2}{} \cdot \ln {K},

where the last step follows from Fact with x = \frac{}{1 - }. To summarize, we have proved:
The number of mistakes made by WMA with parameter \in (0,1) is at most

\frac{2}{1 - } \cdot \mathtt {cost} ^* + \frac{2}{} \cdot \ln {K}.

This bound is very meaningful if \mathtt {cost} ^* is small, but it does not imply sublinear regret guarantees when \mathtt {cost} ^* = \Omega (T). Interestingly, it recovers the O(\ln K) number of mistakes in the special case with a perfect expert, when \mathtt {cost} ^*=0.

Hedge Algorithm
We extend the results from the previous section in two ways: to the general case, online learning with experts, and to o(T) (and, in fact, optimal) regret bounds.

input: What are the limitations of beam modeling in accurately simulating foreground power spectra, and how do uncertainties in beam modeling impact the reliability of these simulations?
expected_output: The limitations of beam modeling in accurately simulating foreground power spectra arise from uncertainties in modeling the beam's angular response and overall gain, particularly at low elevations. The beam models used, such as the full-faceted and perfect paraboloid models, make different assumptions about the dish surface, leading to variations in the simulated foreground power spectra. Additionally, the beam's frequency dependence and chromaticity can cause power to leak into the EOR window, affecting the accuracy of the simulations. These uncertainties impact the reliability of the simulations, as they can result in differences in the predicted amplitude of the pitchfork effect, which is a characteristic feature of the delay spectrum. Furthermore, the beam modeling uncertainties can also affect the sensitivity of the simulations to foreground avoidance and subtraction approaches, leading to variations in the predicted signal-to-noise ratios. Overall, the limitations of beam modeling highlight the need for improved beam modeling techniques and direct measurements to reduce uncertainties and increase the reliability of foreground power spectrum simulations.
context: We consider now the effects of the beam power pattern on the apparent frequency dependence of the foregrounds. discuss the apparent frequency dependence of foregrounds in more detail as well as the contribution from the beam frequency dependence. We focus in this section on the uncertainties in these foreground power spectrum simulations due to beam modeling uncertainties, but first discuss these foreground simulations themselves and their dependence on observing conditions.We simulate foreground power spectra using different primary beam models at various local sidereal times (LSTs). We use frequency-independent model beams (evaluated at 137 MHz) to isolate the interferometric foreground frequency dependence. The added frequency dependence of the changing overall gain and beam shape with frequency is addressed by the other papers in this series. Given that our measured dish power patterns agree well with both numerical models (full-faceted and perfect paraboloid) in the main lobe but deviate in the sidelobes, and that these models make somewhat different assumptions about the dish surface, we take them as a representative pair of possible dish models. We use the empirically best feed height of 5.3 m. We also include the Airy pattern for comparison as in . Beam models with weaker response near the horizon (such as the Airy pattern) downweight sources in this direction of high apparent frequency dependence. This reduces the magnitude of emission near the edge of the EOR window, reducing the risk it leaks inside. We use the per-baseline approach of , by first simulating visibilities measured by specific baselines as a function of frequency, then computing the Fourier transform over frequency (delay transform), and lastly normalizing the result into a cosmological power spectrum following .In detail, we simulate visibilities using the Precision Radio Interferometry Simulatorhttps://github.com/nithyanandan/PRISim (PRISim) for each beam model at various LSTs, modeling the sky as the sum of the Global Sky Model and the NVSS and SUMSS , point source catalogs. We use a frequency spacing of 781 kHz, sufficient to characterize delays within and just outside of the horizon limits on both baseline lengths considered, 14.6 m and 43.8 m. We use a total bandwidth of 100 MHz (effectively reduced to 50 MHz after applying the Blackman-Harris window) centered on 150 MHz. This bandwidth is larger than the 10 MHz thought to be safe from signal evolution with redshift, but is the bandwidth used in the wide band delay space foreground filter of , .Figure REF (top panel) shows simulated foreground delay spectra at various LSTs using the full-faceted beam. As all these LSTs correspond to high galactic latitudes far from the galactic center, the total visibility power (the level of the zero delay mode) varies only by a factor of a few over these LSTs on both baseline lengths (14.6 m (left panel), 43.8 m (right panel)). However the positive delay horizon limit (corresponding to the western horizon) has a peak that varies by over 1.5 orders of magnitude on both baselines, demonstrating the stark difference in horizon brightening when the galaxy is just above versus just below the horizon.

We predict SNRs of 12.7 and 74.3 using foreground avoidance and subtraction approaches respectively, compared with SNRs of 18.7 and 90.8 using an ideal unobstructed 14 m aperture (Airy pattern). Still, these sensitivities permit a very significant detection of the 21 cm signal after a single observing season.Beyond simple sensitivity considerations, though, the beam pattern affects science analyses by reweighting celestial emission in different regions of the sky, which are then imprinted with different frequency dependence by the interferometer. Longer baselines are more susceptible to this effect, giving rise to a “wedge” shaped region in 2D Fourier space. has highlighted that the distribution of foregrounds within the wedge is important as well. If the beam falloff is sufficiently shallow at low elevations, there is a relative brightening of emission from near the horizon in line with the baseline due in part to the large solid angle at low elevations. This produces a characteristic “pitchfork” shape in the delay spectrum of a single baseline, with a zero delay peak due to bright near-zenith emission surrounded by tines at the negative and positive horizon limits due to emission from the two horizon directions in line with the baseline. These horizon peaks are most at risk of leaking foreground power into the EOR window given chromatic instrumental responses such as bandpass miscalibration, though techniques are being developed to suppress emission from near the horizon .We predict the magnitude of this effect for the HERA element and discuss the uncertainties in this estimate due to beam modeling uncertainty. As expected, we find that the level of horizon brightening is largest when the galaxy is just above the horizon, and lowest when it is well below. When this pitchfork effect is large, we find that the uncertainty in its predicted amplitude is also large, as seen in the differences between the delay spectra calculated using full-faceted and perfect paraboloid beam models. When the effect is small, the two beam models produce much more similar results, highlighting the delay spectrum as an exquisite probe of the difficult-to-measure beam response at very low elevations. Of course the delay spectrum provides only an integrated measure of the beam, but some information can still be extracted. By forward modeling foreground delay spectra using different MWA primary beam models, for instance, it was observed that the MWA bowtie dipoles are better modeled as isotropic radiators than hertzian dipoles at these low elevations (N. Thyagarajan, private communication). Direct measurements using transmitter-equipped drones would be ideal and their development is ongoing , .As discussed by the other papers in this series, the frequency dependence of both the beam's angular response and its overall gain widen the delay kernel of a source, leaking power into the EOR window out to {{formula:82b294ac-b609-4e0c-bdf2-59f51d93abe6}} 0.15h Mpc{{formula:a0de4091-8ed5-4dfd-8ea4-874a9e134968}} over much of the 100-200MHz band. This leakage falls within the wedge buffer used in a fiducial foreground avoidance analysis, so our SNR projections take into account the sensitivity reduction due to beam chromaticity. These sensitivities can be improved using new techniques such as foreground covariance downweighting and fringe rate filtering, which mitigate foreground leakage into the EOR window, thereby permitting a smaller buffer.

The space of maximal ideals, denoted as {\cal I}({\cal A}), can be used to define characters as projections, which in turn specify the topology of the algebra. Each character is uniquely specified in the spectrum of the algebra by the maximal ideal, allowing for the definition of the space of characters as the set of projections from the algebra to its quotient spaces with respect to the maximal ideals. This provides a means to construct the topology of the algebra from its maximal ideals, making them a fundamental component in the study of C^* -algebras.

input: Does FAN methodology effectively prevent Dropmark attacks in various scenarios?
expected_output: The FAN methodology can help prevent Dropmark attacks by allowing developers to tighten the tolerance embedded in feature designs, thereby reducing the potential for exploitation. With a FAN architecture, developers can deploy new iterations of functionalities with plugins, programming new behavior as it is needed, without having to consider forward or backward compatibility concerns. This enables the deployment of conservative policies that can make the Dropmark attack unreliable, as demonstrated in the case study. Additionally, the FAN methodology can facilitate the deployment of incentives schemes and path selection performance improvements that require the whole network to be compliant, further enhancing the security of the Tor network. However, it is essential to note that this work assumes trusted plugin developers, and future research is needed to explore the benefits of pushing threat modeling and security concerns to the application layer.

How can RFF kernels be used to effectively address non-Euclidean sequential data in machine learning applications?
expected_output: RFF kernels can be used to effectively address non-Euclidean sequential data in machine learning applications by providing a way to map the sequential data into a higher-dimensional feature space, where the data can be processed using traditional machine learning algorithms. The RFF kernel, defined as $\tilde{\texttt {k}}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}) = \frac{1}{\tilde{d}} \sum _{j=1}^{\tilde{d}} \cos \left( \mathbf {w}_j^\top (\mathbf {x}- \mathbf {y}) \right)$, can be used to capture the geometric structure and symmetries existing within the sequential data. Additionally, the RFF kernel is $\left( \frac{\left\Vert \mathbf {W} \right\Vert _2}{\sqrt{\tilde{d}}} \right)$-Lipschitz, which provides a bound on the difference between the feature maps of two input sequences, allowing for effective processing of sequential data with varying lengths and structures. This makes RFF kernels a useful tool for addressing the challenges of non-Euclidean sequential data, including time-space patterns, time-warping invariance, and discretization and irregular sampling.

Machine learning has successfully been applied to tasks that require learning from complex and structured data types on non-Euclidean domains. Feature engineering on such domains is often tackled by exploiting the geometric structure and symmetries existing within the data .
Learning from sequential data (such as video, text, audio, time series, health data, etc.) is a classic, but an ongoing challenge due to the following properties:Non-Euclidean data. The data domain is nonlinear since there is no obvious and natural way of adding sequences of different length.

Time-space patterns.
Statistically significant patterns can be distributed over time and space, that is, capturing the order structure in which “events” arise is crucial.

Time-warping invariance. The meaning of many sequences is often invariant to reparametrization also frequently called time-warping, at least to an extent; e.g. a sentence spoken quicker or slower contains (essentially) the same information.

Discretization and irregular sampling.
Sequences often arise by sampling along an irregularly spaced grid of an underlying continuous time process. A general methodology should be robust as the sampling gets finer, sequences approximate paths (continuous-time limit), or as the discretization grid varies between sequences.

Scalability. Sequence datasets can quickly become massive, so the computational complexity should grow subquadratically, in terms of all of the state-space dimension, and the length and number of sequences.The signature kernel \texttt {k}_\texttt {Sig} is the state-of-the-art kernel for sequential data, that addresses the first 4 of the above questions and can rely on the modular and powerful framework of kernel learning .
Its construction is motivated by classic ideas from stochastic analysis that give a structured description of a sequence by developing it into a series of tensors.
We refer to for a recent overview of its various constructions and applications.

input: What are the limitations of using dot product similarity in maintaining NTK constancy?
expected_output: The limitations of using dot product similarity in maintaining Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) constancy are significant, as it can lead to cases where the change in weights becomes arbitrarily large even for arbitrarily wide neural networks. This is because the dot product similarity measure does not have normalization, allowing the loss to be minimized arbitrarily by scaling the weights, which in turn causes the weights to grow arbitrarily large with time. As a result, the NTK does not remain constant, and its change can become unbounded as the training time progresses. This phenomenon is demonstrated in the proposition, which shows that for a specific setup with linear activation, gradient flow training, and a particular dataset, the NTK satisfies a condition where its change becomes infinite as the training time approaches a certain value. input: Do the elements in NGC 4372 exhibit intrinsic scatter, and if so, what are the implications for our understanding of this globular cluster?
expected_output: The elements in NGC 4372 do exhibit intrinsic scatter, as evidenced by the comparison between the observed dispersion in chemical abundances and the expected dispersion given by internal errors. When excluding star #7 from the error estimation, a clear intrinsic spread can be identified in the elements O, Na, and Al. This intrinsic scatter suggests that there is a genuine variation in the abundances of these elements among the stars in NGC 4372, rather than the variations being solely due to measurement errors. The presence of intrinsic scatter in these elements has implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of NGC 4372, as it may indicate that the cluster has experienced a complex star formation history, potentially involving multiple generations of stars with different chemical compositions. Additionally, the intrinsic scatter in O, Na, and Al abundances is consistent with the expected signature of material processed during H-burning by high-temperature proton-capture reactions, which is a characteristic feature of globular clusters.

input: What causes priors on θ and α(s) to regularize basis coefficients?
expected_output: The priors on θ and α(s) cause regularization of the basis coefficients because they introduce a penalty term that prevents the basis coefficients from having large values, thereby reducing overfitting. The prior on the basis coefficients θ acts as a regularizer by controlling the magnitude of the coefficients, while the prior on the latent variables α(s) also contributes to regularization by introducing a penalty term that depends on the values of θ and α(s). This is evident from the equation for the variational posterior of θ, which includes the prior terms p(θ | σβ^2) and p(α(s) | θ, σα^2), indicating that the priors on θ and α(s) play a role in regularizing the basis coefficients.

input: What are the differences in collaborative behavior between male and female CS researchers?
expected_output: The differences in collaborative behavior between male and female computer science (CS) researchers are notable. Female researchers tend to have smaller, more closed networks with fewer brokerage opportunities, and their collaborations are more short-lived compared to those of their male counterparts. Additionally, women's networks are more clustered, indicating a stronger emphasis on network closure, whereas men's networks are more open, facilitating the exploration of new knowledge resources and innovation. This division of labor in computer science suggests that women tend to focus on gathering knowledge within tightly-knit communities, while men tend to seek innovations across structural holes. However, it is essential to note that successful female CS researchers exhibit similar collaborative behavior to their successful male colleagues, indicating that the difference in collaboration patterns is not a barrier to success, but rather a difference in the likelihood of adopting these patterns.
context:
To construct a time-evolving collaboration network we use the DBLP Computer Science Bibliography , a comprehensive collection of computer science publications from major and minor journals and conferences. While DBLP offers name disambiguation, it does not provide information about citations. Therefore, we use publication titles to combine the DBLP dataset with the Aminer dataset that contains all citation relations among papers in DBLP.To infer the gender of authors we utilized a method from a previous study that combines the result of name-based (Genderize.iohttps://genderize.io/) and image-based (Face++https://www.faceplusplus.com/) gender detection services . Compared to other name-based methods, our approach achieves a high accuracy (above 90%) for most countries (see Mixed1 in Table REF ). For evaluation we used ground-truth data from a previous study that was manually compiled by looking at the CVs, pictures and institutional websites of a random sample of scientists (693 men and 723 women) .Our combined approach does a better job in inferring non-western names but also performs poorly for Asian (Chinese or Korean) names (see Table REF ).
Therefore, we first detect which names are Asian and label their gender as “unknown”.
The authors for which we cannot detect the gender are excluded from our gender-specific analyses, but included in all structural analyses (e.g., as alters).To detect Chinese names we compile a list of 202,045 unique names from the China Biographical Database Project (CBDB)http://projects.iq.harvard.edu/cbdb/home. For compiling a list of Korean names we use Wikipedia as our data source. To do this, we extract the page titles of all the backlinks to the Wikipedia page “Korean names”https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_name. The page titles include the names of prominent Korean figures (e.g., singers) with a Wikipedia page that describe the origin of the name of that person (e.g., Wikipedia page of a Korean singer and actorhttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahn_Jae-wook). Using this method we compile a list of 6,451 unique Korean names.
A manual evaluation of our Asian name detector shows that 88 out of 100 randomly selected scientists were correctly classified; we found 20 true positives (Asians classified as Asians), 68 true negatives (Non-Asians classified as Non-Asians), 2 false negatives (Asians classified as Non-Asians) and 10 false positives (Non-Asians classified as Asians). The relatively high number of false positives can be explained by the fact that some famous Asians choose western names.
In addition, we exclude authors with only first initials since we cannot infer the gender of authors without knowing their first name. This may exclude female authors disproportionately, particularly in early decades when women may have been more likely than men to publish with initials to avoid potential discrimination. But we expect that this difference is small since our data collection only goes back to 1970.

A potential gender gap in academia, especially in STEM fields, has been a great concern over the past decades and many studies have tried to quantify the extent to which gender inequalities are present in science.In this study, we have focused on the collaborative behaviour of scientists in one entire scientific field, computer science, a densifying field with a collaborative style and a wide gender gap .
We have taken a career approach and analyzed how male and female scientists differ in their dropout rates, their productivity, their tendency to associate with same-sex researchers as well as their collaborative behaviour and its relation with success in academia.We find that the dropout rate of women in computer science is consistently higher than of men. Women also have smaller probabilities to continue after their first publication year, enter early- and mid-career stages and become senior researchers.
Controlling for this difference in careers is our solution to the productivity puzzle that women have a smaller publication output than men. The solution is found in a strong correlation between the productivity gap and what we call the seniority gap. Put simply, men are more productive on average because they have a larger fraction of senior authors. We solve this puzzle without the need to refer to exogenous factors or use other sources but bibliographic data, .There is no gender effect regarding success. Women are more likely to have a larger {{formula:b1ae6349-a0c3-4906-bf3f-6550c5187e3e}} -index than men, but the gender variable does not interact with any of the collaboration features. Structural insights from regressions of success on collaborative patterns over researchers' careers are more revealing. They show that network closure and network brokerage are co-determinants of citation impact or the {{formula:f24ada3b-969f-43cd-8c73-280e0f51585a}} -index.
Successful scientists embed in large networks and build trustful relationships through repeating collaborations throughout their careers . But, at the same time, successful scientists also bridge structural holes to exploit various knowledge resources and stay innovative, making brokerage and closure a true duality , . This resonates with theories in the sociology of science that tradition and innovation is the “essential tension” in scientific research , or in organization science that the exploration of new possibilities necessarily complements the exploitation of old certainties .Interestingly, our temporal classification of gender on collaborative behaviour demonstrates that male and female researchers do embed into different ego networks on average. “Female” networks are significantly smaller, much more closed (clustered), contain fewer brokerage opportunities and are more short-lived (regarding median collaboration durations) than those of men. Controlling for dynamic effects and career ages, there is a division of labour in computer science: Women tend to take care of network closure and gather knowledge in tightly-knit communities while men tend to hunt for innovations across structural holes.
Related disparities have been observed in managerial networks where women are more successful with a small network of interconnected contacts or where trustful relations and group reproduction have been found to increase with the presence of women .While the difference in network structure for men and women opens up future venues of research into potential gender gaps in science, it is not in conflict with our results that there are no gender-specific differences in how collaboration patterns impact success.The suggested solution to the seeming paradox is that women are on average less likely to adapt the collaboration patterns that are related with success. However, those women who become successful computer scientists exhibit the same collaborative behaviour as their successful male colleagues.Regarding the mixing of men and women over time we find that gender homophily has been increasing ever since.

input: What are the limitations of classical PAC bounds when applied to over-parameterized neural networks?
expected_output: Classical PAC bounds have limitations when applied to over-parameterized neural networks, as the complexity of these networks is often large, being exponential in depth or linear in the number of parameters. This results in classical bounds becoming too loose or even vacuous in the over-parameterized setting, failing to explain the generalization ability of neural networks. The high complexity of the model class relative to the volume of training data allows the model to fit the training data perfectly but fail to generalize to test data, leading to a mismatch between empirical observations and classical theory.
context:
Classical PAC learning theory balances model complexity (the expressiveness of a model class) against data volume. When a model class is too expressive relative to the volume of training data, it has the ability to ace the training data while flunking the test data, and learning fails.
Classical theory fails to explain generalization in over-parameterized neural nets, as the complexity of networks is often large (exponential in depth [, ] or linear in the number of parameters [, ]). Therefore classical bounds become too loose or even vacuous in the over-parameterized setting that we are interested in studying.To explain this mismatch between empirical observation and classical theory, a number of recent works propose new metrics that characterize the capacity of neural networks.
Most of these appeal to the PAC framework to characterize the generalization ability of a model class {{formula:e8c0da2e-f6c9-45b8-bb90-5487f78f3c50}} (e.g., neural nets of a shared architecture) through a high probability upper bound: with probability at least {{formula:503f328d-da47-411e-a870-f7e9458f38dd}} ,

Such bounds can improve the model class complexity provided that weight matrices adhere to some structural constraints (e.g. sparsity or eigenvalue concentration).Stability and robustness. This line of work considers {{formula:4a497db7-e9df-494f-9f9e-ac4c0628485d}} to be proportional to the stability of the model (, ), which is a measure of how much changing a data point in {{formula:58a4f1f2-075a-4050-bbe1-fde54e401d4c}} changes the output of the model (). However it is nontrivial to characterize the stability of a neural network. Robustness, while producing insightful and effective generalization bounds, still suffers from the curse of the dimensionality on the priori-known fixed input manifold.PAC-Bayes and margin theory. PAC-Bayes bounds (, ), provide generalization guarantees for randomized predictors drawn from a learned distribution that depends on the training data, as opposed to a learned single predictor.

input: What is the effect of void fraction on transmission probability in a given system?
expected_output: The effect of void fraction on transmission probability in the given system is that the transmission probability increases with the void fraction. This is because for large values of void fraction, the medium is prevalently composed of voids, which enhances transmission by allowing particle trajectories to pass through with fewer collisions. Conversely, when the void fraction decreases, the proportion of scattering material increases, leading to a higher probability of particles scattering, changing direction, and leaking from the face where the source is imposed, thereby reducing transmission.

input: Does increased model complexity actually improve the accuracy of the H i size-mass relation?
expected_output: The increased model complexity does not necessarily improve the accuracy of the H i size-mass relation, as the results show that all three analytic profiles generally reflect the shape of the TNG100 profiles, with model 3 having the lowest scatter in the residuals, but the returned H i mass values for the model-3 fits are the least faithful to the true values for both simulations. In fact, the results indicate that model 1 provides the most accurate returned H i mass values, suggesting that increased complexity does not always lead to improved accuracy. Additionally, the overall scatter in the model-1 fits is lower for Dark Sage, further supporting the idea that increased model complexity does not necessarily improve the accuracy of the H i size-mass relation.
context:

For each model, we show an example {{formula:ffb71b11-e17a-4e37-ab5d-75389c42f78e}}  profile in Fig. REF , which is accompanied by a real example galaxy whose observed H i surface density profile is well described by that model. We will show that regardless of how much detail is added to the disc profiles, one can always mathematically derive a tight H i size–mass relation that matches observations. Nevertheless, all three analytic profiles generally reflect the shape of TNG100 profiles, with model 3 edging model 2 for the lowest scatter in the residuals, and models 3 and 1 each giving twice the number of lowest-{{formula:56afbcc1-c30c-4eff-867a-db42c09dba31}} fits than model 2. input: How do synthetic photometry and flux calibration estimate source magnitudes?
expected_output: Synthetic photometry and flux calibration estimate source magnitudes by convolving spectra with standard imaging filters, such as the Johnson-Cousins UBVRI filters and the 2MASS JHK filters, to obtain spectrophotometric magnitudes. The precision of this procedure is tested by flux calibrating telluric standard stars and comparing their measured magnitudes to their archival Simbad magnitudes, which yields a dispersion of 0.1 magnitudes. This value is used as an estimate of the error in the procedure. Additionally, an offset of 0.3 magnitudes is found between the archival and measured magnitudes in certain filters, which is subtracted from the measured values to obtain the final magnitudes. The final error on the magnitude is estimated to be 0.15 magnitude, which is the quadratic sum of the dispersion and the offset.
context:
We estimated the magnitudes of the sources by performing synthetic photometry on our spectra. We convolved our spectra with standard imaging filters, namely the Johnson-Cousins UBVRI filters and the 2MASS JHK{{formula:144e4f4d-135e-473b-879e-6796afa88369}} filters. The filters parameters were taken from the ADPS web siteAsiago Database on Photometric Systems, http://ulisse.pd.astro.it/Astro/ADPS/Systems/index.html.To test the precision of our procedure, we flux calibrated the telluric standard stars and computed their spectrophotometric magnitudes as we did for the science targets. We then compared this result to their Simbad magnitudes. The difference between archival and measured magnitudes had a dispersion of 0.1 magnitudes (1{{formula:c0981d97-6b3c-40e2-9ef4-3422261bf59f}} ) in all filters, we therefore used this value as an estimate of the error in our procedure. Moreover, we found an offset of {{formula:f7803096-b33b-4633-87f9-88873791f907}} 0.3 {{formula:bce97e59-63a8-4055-a08c-fdf1f941e6ea}} 0.1 magnitudes between the archival and the measured magnitudes in the {{formula:63b5e0ab-ad4f-4d2e-9604-b0599957b62a}} and {{formula:d63919ce-11a4-4162-a7cb-44c544395525}} filters. This offset tends to zero towards longer wavelengths. As we used the UVB arm to set the flux scale, we subtracted this offset to our measured values. The final error on the magnitude was {{formula:6ce7bd3f-e71d-4d99-95fc-549b8f254c60}} {{formula:f3d86bf3-652f-4f96-9b90-0e999e01c0ff}} 0.15 magnitude; this is the quadratic sum of the two estimates discussed above. The results are in Table REF , along with the 2MASS survey magnitudes. During our observations, PKS 0447–439 was about 1.5 magnitude brighter than in the 2MASS survey, while PKS 0301–243 was about 1 magnitude brighter. All the other sources magnitudes can be found within half a magnitude from the 2MASS values.
[Table: List of the strongest emission or absorption lines.]

In the optical-ultraviolet range, the observed SED of a blazar is a combination of jet emission, AGN activity (thermal and non-thermal), and thermal emission of the host galaxy, which usually is an elliptical . Depending on the relative strength of each component, the spectrum might be featureless, or it may display signatures coming from the host galaxy. This is clearly shown in the simulations performed by and . We modelled the emission using a combination of a power law (featureless continuum) with the local elliptical template of by adding Gaussian emission features when needed. The fit was performed via a {{formula:24106191-58a4-466e-bde8-d501f50151a0}} minimisation using the MINUIT packagehttp://root.cern.ch/root/html/TMinuit.html.The free parameters of the model are the power law wavelength index, its normalisation at 10000 Å and the flux level at 10000 Å of the host galaxy emission. If the redshift was previously determined by the detection of a feature, the fit was performed at that redshift, thereby allowing us to estimate the flux of the host galaxy. The statistical errors provided by the fitting method are in general unphysically small (typically {{formula:1f2aa9bc-f863-46e1-b864-971a8bb137cc}} times lower than the fitted value). Therefore, by following the approach of , we independently fitted separated sections of the spectra and estimated the error from the differences between the resulting parameters.When no feature (or only an intervening absorption system) was detected, we fitted the spectrum with a simple power law with a normalisation at 10000 Å as above and we estimated the fitting errors in the same way. We also estimated a lower limit on the redshift with the imaging method of using a host galaxy magnitude {{formula:58714732-fc95-4946-9551-bf09f722a7fa}} . Moreover, to estimate an upper limit to the galaxy contribution, we constructed a grid of blazar emission models at the redshift of the farthest absorbing system (if present) or at the redshift determined with the imaging method. These models were built as the sum of the measured power law and of a template with growing flux to which we added Poissonian noise to achieve the signal-to-noise of our observations. For each model in the grid, we measured the EW of the Ca II H&K feature, which is the first to be clearly visible at these redshifts. The upper limit was fixed when the feature was detected at the 2 {{formula:c2e88db7-fd83-4d8a-80d0-7242514ba392}} level. In one case, namely for PKS 0301–243, we used published photometry of the host galaxy to estimate the flux of the template; the upper limit to the template flux was determined as discussed above. To account for the emission lines detected in two cases, we added narrow lines with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 500 km/s to the template, which are compatible with central gas dispersion in local galaxies . This allowed a rough estimation of the line ratios in these objects.Results are given in Table REF for sources for which we determined a firm redshift and in Table REF for the others.

In contrast, the completions K_v of K are complete with respect to their respective absolute values, but they do not necessarily have a compact topology. The embedding of K into AK allows for a comparison of their topological properties, with AK providing a more comprehensive and compact representation of the various completions of K.

input: What mathematical principles underlie the quasi-steady-state approximation in Michaelis-Menten reactions?
expected_output: The quasi-steady-state approximation (QSSA) in Michaelis-Menten reactions is underpinned by mathematical principles related to timescale separation and the concept of a slow manifold. The work of Segel and Segel and Slemrod provides the foundation for understanding the timescales and criterion for the validity of the QSSA. Furthermore, the research of Roussel and Fraser offers a geometrical argument for the global validity of the QSSA, highlighting the importance of approximating the slow manifold to a high degree of accuracy. Their work demonstrates that a specific condition is necessary for the long-time validity of the QSSA, thereby providing a deeper quantitative understanding of the QSSA in the context of Michaelis-Menten reaction mechanisms.
context:
In this section we review the application of the different versions of the QSSA
for the MM reaction mechanism (REF ), and the mathematical justification for
the application of each approximation. We also present the timescales
and criterion for the validity of the QSSA originally derived by Segel 
and Segel and Slemrod .

Even though timescale separation is quite large, there are regions in the numerically-obtained time course data where c ε T c^{\varepsilon _T} approximates cc only to within one digit of accuracy. While the loss in accuracy may not be outright disastrous in terms of parameter estimation, it is an observation that is worth pointing out in order to gain a deeper quantitative understanding of the various QSS approximations utilized for Michaelis–Menten reaction mechanism (). The parameters have been assigned arbitrary units for illustrative purposes.]Roussel and Fraser  seem to have been the first to really understand this in the context of the Michaelis–Menten reaction mechanism (REF ), as their work focused on approximating the actual invariant slow manifold. In fact, to the best of the authors' knowledge, Roussel and Fraser (see , pp. 42-47) were the first to provide a solid geometrical argument that {{formula:84bdaf1a-73ce-49ab-92c1-c8015a1ff14d}} is in fact the “global" qualifier for the validity of the sQSSA instead of {{formula:1f638788-ba88-4025-977c-a3b9ccca0cb1}} . By approximating the slow manifold to a high degree of accuracy, Roussel and Fraser , were able to demonstrate that {{formula:c2aefe64-7cd4-4b6b-93fe-2287f5160d29}} is necessary for the long-time validity of the sQSSA.

input: Does GS outperform other metrics in manifold approximation accuracy via topological loop counts?
expected_output: GS does not necessarily outperform other metrics in manifold approximation accuracy via topological loop counts, as it is strictly sensitive to the topology of the loop structures and is insensitive to differences in relative embedding distances or orientations within the manifold. The authors acknowledge this limitation and recommend using GS in conjunction with other metrics to achieve more comprehensive results.
context: The topological relationships are extracted in terms of the counts of 1-dimensional loops in a graph structure built up from proximity relationships as a distance threshold is increased. Although it may be indirectly sensitive to variations in the dimensionality of the manifolds, GS explicitly rewards only matches in terms of the specific topology of these loop structures in approximations of the manifolds. However, due to its strictly topological nature, GS is insensitive to differences in relative embedding distances or orientations within the manifold. This issue is acknowledged by the authors, who advise that GS would be best suited for use in conjunction with other metrics .

input: What causes the particle Langevin algorithm to be inefficient when there is uncontrolled error in log posterior density gradient estimation?
expected_output: The particle Langevin algorithm is asymptotically no more efficient than the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm when there is no control over errors in the estimate of the gradient of the log posterior density, indicating that uncontrolled error in log posterior density gradient estimation is the primary cause of inefficiency in the particle Langevin algorithm.
context:
Our theory identifies three
distinct asymptotic regimes corresponding to three different ranges
of control over errors in the estimate of the gradient of the
log posterior density. We have shown that, if there is no control of these errors, then the particle Langevin algorithm is asymptotically no more
efficient than the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm. By contrast, if there is
sufficient control, the particle
Langevin algorithm attains the same asymptotic advantage in
efficiency over the particle random-walk algorithm as the Metropolis
adjusted Langevin algorithm enjoys over its random-walk Metropolis counterpart.In the preferred regime, and specifically when the estimate of the
log posterior density is generated by a particle filter, we identify an
optimal variance for the error in the log posterior density of approximately
{{formula:aae8703e-6a70-4f45-aef5-159756c32f45}} and an optimal
acceptance rate of approximately {{formula:3563c641-c55a-4478-88da-cd2c1be10574}} . We also find that the optimal scaling is insensitive
to the choice of variance and vice-versa. In general, however, the regime is not known, and so,
conditional on a fixed but arbitrary
number of particles, we provide a mechanism for tuning the scaling of
the proposal by aiming for a maximin acceptance rate that is
robust to the regime. This ensures that the resulting algorithm will
achieve at least {{formula:d200adea-8f3e-46e5-a9ab-2116a867d4a1}} of the efficiency that it would were the regime known and
the best scaling for that regime chosen.Our results are the latest in a number of results concerning at optimal
implementations of pseudo-marginal and particle Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, . Using similar techniques
to those in this article, 
identified an optimal variance of {{formula:dbe3f20e-3d74-4fff-9a2a-44c93b95b6a8}} for the target density in the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm, and found that the optimal variance is insensitive to the scaling and
vice-versa. analyzed non-asymptotic bounds on the integrated

{{formula:25612092-3661-4eb0-a282-26b5e8d3c932}} , also suggesting an insensitivity. In high dimensions,
one should tune to the variance suggested by the asymptotic theory, but

is typically less than 3.
