REF . For the second strategy, start with a sensible scaling, find the number of
particles that optimizes the overall efficiency, for example effective sample size per second, then with
this number of particles, find
the scaling which optimizes efficiency, for example effective sample size.

We simulate from the posterior density {{formula:4aa113b4-05bd-432e-b2f4-8d066982b421}} using
the pseudo-marginal algorithm where the likelihood
is estimated using the bootstrap particle filter with {{formula:4c626924-afac-4a52-a8fd-77c7772e85fe}} particles. A
multivariate Student-t random walk proposal on the parameter components transformed to
the real line is used.

input: What conditions ensure 2nd order differentiability of semi-discrete optimal transport distance?
expected_output: The conditions that ensure 2nd order differentiability of semi-discrete optimal transport distance involve an arbitrary cost with respect to the locations of the Dirac masses, allowing for more general background measures than the typical densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This is achieved by utilizing the framework developed by Kitagawa and Mérigot, which overcomes previous restrictions and provides a proof of existence, unlike earlier work by De Goes that only provided a formula for the Hessian in the Euclidean setting without proving its existence.
context:
Optimal transport , is a blossoming subject that has known major breakthroughs these last decades. Its applications range from finance , mesh generation , PDE analysis and imaging , to machine learning and clustering , .This paper is limited to the semi-discrete case, which consists in transporting discrete measures (Dirac masses) towards a background measure. However we allow more general background measures than the densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure that are usually found in the literature. In this setting, we prove second order differentiability of the optimal transport distance for an arbitrary cost with respect to the locations of the Dirac masses.Precursors include De Goes (Proposition 2.5.4) who has given the formula of the Hessian in the Euclidean setting. However he has given no proof of existence. We will make use of the framework developed by Kitagawa and Mérigot to overcome these restrictions.As a by-product, we obtain the second order differentiability conditions for the so-called energy of a Voronoi diagram.
The latter remark generalizes results presented in , to higher dimensions and lower regularity of the background measure.

The goal of this section is to show the convergence of the Damped
Newton algorithm for semi-discrete optimal transport. This follows in
fact from a more general result. We establish in Section
REF the convergence of the damped
Newton algorithm (Algorithm REF ) under general
assumptions on the functional. We finally apply this algorithm to the
semi-discrete optimal transport problem, using the intermediate
results (regularity and strict concavity of the Kantorovich
functional) proven in
Section  and .

input: How do adversarial masks compare to smooth masks in terms of their impact on classifier predictions?
expected_output: Adversarial masks have a significantly greater impact on classifier predictions compared to smooth masks, as they can introduce a large amount of additional evidence by generating adversarial artifacts that are very small in magnitude and almost imperceivable for humans, but can completely destroy the original prediction of the classifier. In contrast, smooth masks are less likely to introduce such artifacts and therefore have a lesser impact on classifier predictions. The use of adversarial masks can result in poor saliency explanations, whereas smooth masks are generally more desirable as they do not introduce unwanted evidence. Additionally, techniques such as applying a mask that selectively adds blur to the image can make it harder to generate high-frequency-high-evidence artifacts, thereby reducing the impact of adversarial masks on classifier predictions.
context:
As mentioned in the previous section, by manipulating the image we always introduce some extra evidence. Here, let us focus on the case of applying a mask {{formula:f9d6a797-6dbf-48cc-bbb0-72cbf20d8e84}} to the image {{formula:c66bf42d-7977-4fce-90d7-b4aaee0a9816}} to obtain the edited image {{formula:9ee01d28-3d2c-4eef-8370-59664b14e471}} . In the simplest case we can simply multiply {{formula:f9fbbd86-f024-4a1e-8ca7-6926f15536c4}} and {{formula:0c4cf58d-35e7-4198-90ae-858fce83be4a}} element-wise:
{{formula:1c00aa12-66e7-4421-a1be-e11abc3497a2}}This operation sets certain regions of the image to a constant “0” colour. While setting a larger patch of the image to “0” may sound rather harmless (perhaps following the assumption that the mean of all colors carries very little evidence), we may encounter problems when the mask {{formula:3997b500-b8a3-488f-81c5-976a8324910f}} is not smooth. The mask {{formula:2b99b7ed-1340-4613-88b2-d18643561cae}} , in the worst case, can be used to introduce a large amount of additional evidence by generating adversarial artifacts (a similar observation was made in ). An example of such a mask is presented in figure REF . Adversarial artifacts generated by the mask are very small in magnitude and almost imperceivable for humans, but they are able to completely destroy the original prediction of the classifier. Such adversarial masks provide very poor saliency explanations and therefore should be avoided.
[Figure: The adversarial mask introduces very small perturbations, but can completely alter the classifier's predictions. From left to right: an image which is correctly recognised by the classifier with a high confidence as a "tabby cat"; a generated adversarial mask; an original image after application of the mask that is no longer recognised as a "tabby cat".]There are a few ways to make the introduction of artifacts harder. For example, we may change the way we apply a mask to reduce the amount of unwanted evidence due to specifically-crafted masks:
{{formula:fe9205e3-5d04-41eb-9258-66d3f22dd488}}where {{formula:b7941ce6-62a5-4eac-97b4-5dee00005395}} is an alternative image. {{formula:79b414f2-d686-4067-b9cc-f335849efa92}} can be chosen to be for example a highly blurred version of {{formula:15170b75-8a8e-4a2f-9fb2-194b9233180a}} . In such case mask {{formula:babe904e-af86-4c9d-9636-98efcb9f6b98}} simply selectively adds blur to the image {{formula:6d2ee07b-e343-43b9-86c0-6a75f78c8924}} and therefore it is much harder to generate high-frequency-high-evidence artifacts.

Answering the “what” question means describing the properties of the mapping {{formula:d0b7d28b-921c-4aaa-8fdd-001e9f819c97}} . For example, a classifier {{formula:5e70a930-d414-4c07-a728-4eea558a4aef}} is often characterized in terms of its expected error rate. Other characterizations include: whether {{formula:58623a5f-17d6-4ea1-8c05-4742441573fd}} is invariant with a viewpoint change, if there are intra-class variations of the object that may confuse {{formula:b2b231bf-0f31-46e4-a65a-855e0dc82d36}} , if {{formula:d5297a71-c8ef-4f4e-a156-b59e9151fbc0}} recognizes the object by using contextual cues, and so on. Answering the “how” question means clarifying which computational mechanisms are used by {{formula:3bd835c0-b193-42f8-b60d-5c9399a66f32}} in order to achieve such properties.While the discussion has so far been informal, the next section attempts to formalize these concepts, focusing on the “what” question.

input: What are the advantages of Adam over SGD in minimizing cross-entropy loss?
expected_output: The Adam optimizer performed better than stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in minimizing cross-entropy loss, as it made faster progress in terms of both the number of iterations and wall-clock time. Additionally, Adam outperformed other methods, including the sum-of-functions (SFO) method, in training multi-layer neural networks, especially when using dropout stochastic regularization. This is because Adam is more effective in handling non-convex objective functions and can adapt to different learning rates for different parameters, such as the pulse spike time and the weights of both pulse and non-pulse neurons. Overall, Adam's advantages over SGD include its ability to converge faster and more effectively, even in the presence of stochastic regularization, making it a more suitable choice for training complex neural networks.
context:
We trained fully connected feedforward networks with topology
n_hidden (a vector of hidden layer sizes). We used Adam
optimization  with mini-batches of size batch_size
to minimise the cross-entropy loss. The Adam optimizer performed better than
stochastic gradient descent. We used different learning rates for the pulse
spike time (learning_rate_pulses) and the weights of both pulse and
non-pulse neurons (learning_rate). We used a fixed firing threshold
(fire_threshold) and decay constant (decay_constant).Network weight initialisation is crucial for the subsequent training of the
network. In a spiking network, it is important that the initial weights are
large enough to cause at least some of the neurons to spike; in absence of
spike events, there will be no gradient to use for learning. We therefore used
a modified form of Glorot initialization  where the weights
are drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation {{formula:69c74688-9d73-4f7a-9459-fcd969dd7051}} (as in the original scheme) and custom
mean {{formula:7a436eda-5c90-4392-9040-b6ee1fc33ccb}} . If the multiplication factor of
the mean is 0, this is the same is the original Glorot initialization scheme.
We set different multiplication factors for pulse
(pulse_init_multiplier), and non-pulse
(nonpulse_init_multiplier) weights. This allows the two types of
neurons to pre-specialise into inhibitory and excitatory roles. In biological
brains, internal oscillations are thought to be generated through inhibitory
activities that regulate the excitatory effects of incoming stimuli
 , .
[Table: Hyperparameters of the model. The first column shows the default parameterschosen to solve Boolean logic problems. The second column shows the searchrange used in the hyperparameter search. Asterisks ( * ^*) mark ranges thatwere probed according to a logarithmic scale; all others were probedlinearly. The last column shows the value chosen from these ranges to solveMNIST.]Despite careful initialisation, the network might still become quiescent during
training. We prevent this problem by adding a fixed small penalty
(penalty_no_spike) to the derivative of all presynaptic weights of a
neuron that has not fired. In practice, after the training phase, some of the
neurons will spike too late to matter in the classification and thus they do
need to spike at all.Another problem is that the gradients become very large as a spike becomes
closer to, but not sufficient for the postsynaptic neuron to reach the firing
threshold. In this case, in Eq. REF  and REF , the value of the
Lambert {{formula:787b8032-1f7c-409b-b8b9-2fb782fc65ee}} function will approach its minimum ({{formula:0d50c3fb-4c66-4b12-a09a-4b7973c475e4}} ) as its argument
approaches {{formula:b8ffa1ef-3df9-4ef1-a3bf-1abb234f6bf7}} , the denominator of the derivatives will approach zero and
the derivatives will approach infinity. To counter this, we clip the
derivatives to a fixed value clip_derivative. Note that this
behaviour will occur in any activation function that has a maximum (hence, a
biologically-plausible shape), is differentiable, and has a continuous
derivative.In addition to these hyperparameters, we explored several other heuristics for
the spiking net.

Multi-layer neural network are powerful models with non-convex objective
functions. Although our convergence analysis does not apply to non-convex
problems, we empirically found that Adam often outperforms other methods in such cases. In our experiments, we
made model choices that are consistent with previous publications in the
area; a neural network model with two fully connected hidden layers with 1000
hidden units each and ReLU activation are used for this experiment with
minibatch size of 128.First, we study different optimizers using the standard deterministic
cross-entropy objective function with {{formula:e35b31e1-300a-4261-9f0f-4474c3a57157}} weight decay on the parameters to
prevent over-fitting.
The sum-of-functions (SFO) method  is a recently proposed quasi-Newton method that works with minibatches of data and has shown good performance on optimization of
multi-layer neural networks. We used their implementation and compared with
Adam to train such models. Figure REF shows that Adam makes faster progress in terms of both the number of iterations and wall-clock time. Due to the cost of updating curvature information, SFO is 5-10x slower per iteration
compared to Adam, and has a memory requirement that is linear in the number minibatches.
[Figure: Training of multilayer neural networks on MNIST images.(a) Neural networks using dropout stochastic regularization. (b)Neural networks with deterministic cost function. We compare withthe sum-of-functions (SFO) optimizer]Stochastic
regularization methods, such as dropout, are an effective way to prevent
over-fitting and often used in practice due to their simplicity. SFO assumes deterministic subfunctions, and indeed failed to
converge on cost functions with stochastic regularization. We
compare the effectiveness of Adam to other stochastic first order methods on
multi-layer neural networks trained with dropout noise. Figure
REF shows our results; Adam shows better convergence than
other methods.

input: What is the implication of approximability on fixed-parameter tractability in computational complexity theory?
expected_output: The implication of approximability on fixed-parameter tractability in computational complexity theory is that the existence of an EPTAS (arbitrarily precise polynomial-time approximation algorithm) directly implies fixed-parameter tractability. Additionally, a constant-factor approximation often forms a starting point for proving fixed-parameter tractability, highlighting a close connection between approximability and the existence of algorithms parameterized by the solution size.
context:
We are interested in approximation algorithms for problems such as the Maximum Independent Set
and its variants (weighted, distance-{{formula:916e7c0e-3172-4a82-89b0-4e8ab266d9e1}} independent for a fixed parameter {{formula:71495932-7620-46d9-a9ed-be7732d201cf}} , ...),
Maximum Induced Matching, Maximum 3-Colorable Induced Subgraph, and similar.
There are many strong non-approximation results that preclude the existence of constant-factor
approximation algorithms for these problems in general; for example, it is NP-hard to
approximate the independence number  of an {{formula:37d6d4cd-3b6d-4c81-abaf-ede992edfd47}} -vertex graph up to the factor of {{formula:a864de6f-37c6-4ba4-b782-e47d92e472fe}} for
every {{formula:0c8ae786-4199-4f57-ba5f-f528cd9a5939}} . Hence, we need to consider more restricted settings.There is a close connection between approximability and the existence of algorithms parameterized by the solution size.
Indeed, the existence of an EPTAS (arbitrarily precise polynomial-time approximation algorithm such that the degree
of the polynomial bounding the complexity does not depend on the precision) directly implies fixed-parameter tractability,
and a constant-factor approximation often forms a starting point for proving fixed-parameter tractability.
A natural family of problems, namely those expressible in the first-order logic, is known to be fixed-parameter tractable
in a subgraph-closed class of graphs if and (under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions) only if
the class is nowhere-dense . Moreover, in a slightly more restrictive setting of
classes with bounded expansion, the parameterized algorithms have linear time complexity .
We refer the reader not familiar with the concept of bounded expansion to Section REF ;
here, let us just mention that examples of graph classes with this property are
planar graphs and more generally all proper minor-closed classes, all graph
classes with bounded maximum degree, and even more generally, graph classes
closed under topological minors, as well as almost all Erdős-Rényi random
graphs with bounded average degree.Motivated by this connection, we explore the approximability of maximization problems expressible in the first-order logic
when restricted to classes with bounded expansion. As our first main result, we show that every monotone
maximization problems expressible in the first-order logic admits a constant-factor approximation algorithm
in every class of graphs of bounded expansion, even in the weighted setting. We need a few definitions to formulate the precise statement.Let {{formula:e873d8d0-6b14-4d2f-9cb1-eec494873626}} be a finite index set and let {{formula:da68a0fc-ebf3-4622-b9a3-13a4626e6108}} be a set of vertices of a graph {{formula:67252b68-eedb-4afb-8347-9c0fb8e181de}} .

The notion of a class of graphs of bounded expansion was
introduced by Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez in  and
in the series of journal papers, .
Examples of classes of graphs
with bounded expansion include proper minor-closed classes of graphs,
classes of graphs with bounded maximum degree, classes of graphs excluding
a subdivision of a fixed graph, classes of graphs that can be embedded
on a fixed surface with bounded number of crossings per edge and
many others, see . Many structural and algorithmic properties
generalize from proper minor-closed classes of graphs to classes
of graphs with bounded expansion, see , .Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez  defined
a class {{formula:e8d2d0aa-c56d-49a8-8377-607a33a5e5a9}} of graphs to be nowhere-dense if
for every {{formula:1e65d874-d83d-417e-9895-72bce7b5550a}} and every integer {{formula:2d2f3a81-2fc7-402d-839d-fd47ebaae10a}} there exists a real number {{formula:56ff46af-7e4d-466f-b07a-417af0907e91}} 
such that if {{formula:b82cf98f-a445-406b-96e3-e68e0ea1efd0}} is an {{formula:5ae1bb68-d14b-4f9e-bcb2-1942bfb9b76d}} -shallow minor of a member of {{formula:223e82c3-d71e-4b76-a532-418e79f91010}} , then
{{formula:9d7a393f-14fa-4572-bff5-9d04ec34c002}} .
(It follows from  that this definition is
indeed equivalent to the one given in .)
It can be shown that every class of graphs with (locally) bounded expansion is
nowhere-dense ,
but the converse is false: the class {{formula:dee425d6-9f07-49bc-a692-51f0a4a1227b}} of graphs {{formula:05213d75-e500-467c-ac56-d8c656b85808}} with no cycles of length
less than {{formula:1b57c9ec-43ca-4625-bb53-57b0c1310f19}} is nowhere-dense but it fails to have bounded expansion;

input: Does adding noninteracting qubits actually protect Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) in quantum systems?
expected_output: According to the context, adding noninteracting qubits to a common dissipative reservoir can completely protect the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. The results show that increasing the number of additional qubits can lead to the protection of QFI, and the behavior of QFI can exhibit either monotonic decay or non-monotonic behavior with revival oscillations, depending on the number of additional qubits. This suggests that the addition of noninteracting qubits can have a positive effect on the protection of QFI in quantum systems.
context:
Though some recent works are based on the environment effects on the QFI dynamics of the open system in the weak coupling regime, there are still some interesting results that need further discussion and in-depth study. In this paper, we study the QFI for a single-qubit system coupled to a common dissipative reservoirs through the addition qubits into reservoir. We mainly focus on the influence of the additional noninteracting qubits on the QFI dynamics. The results show that, the QFI is completely protected in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes by increasing the number of additional qubits. Besides, the phenomena of QFI display monotonic decay or non-monotonic with revival oscillations depending on the number of additional qubits {{formula:400ec653-dd5a-4982-a4ed-f1a5a649259e}} in a common dissipative reservoir. If {{formula:b3fb9add-1038-4f65-9109-2e9e61cb7070}} , the behavior of QFI with monotonic decay occurs. However, if {{formula:16e77c87-0170-429a-9cdb-a890aee05b3c}} , QFI exhibits non-monotonic behavior with revival oscillations for whatever system-reservoir coupling strengths. Moreover, we extend this model to investigate the effect of the addition of qubits and the initial conditions of the system on the GP. The GP for a nonunitary evolving qubit is calculated according to the formula of Ref. , we find that, the GP is unaffected by the dissipative reservoir with the number of additional qubits increasing, regardless of whether the qubit system is in Markovian or non-Markovian regimes. However, the GP is sensitive to the initial parameter {{formula:a4ce8a20-fc1b-40e3-9df7-ed1d66eaa961}} , and possesses symmetric in a range regime {{formula:3aabb407-2c00-4b6f-88c5-9d0724082843}} .This research is supported by the Start-up Funds for Talent Introduction and Scientific Research of Changsha University 2015 (Grant No.SF1504), the Scientific Research Project of Hunan Province Department of Education (Grant Nos.16C0134 and 17C0133), the Natural Science Foundation of Hunan Province (Grant No.2017JJ3346), Key Laboratory of Low-Dimensional Quantum Structures and

A kinematic approach to the geometric phase for mixed quantal states
in nonunitary evolution is proposed. This phase is manifestly gauge
invariant and can be experimentally tested in interferometry. It leads
to well-known results when the evolution is unitary.

03.65.Vf

The concept of geometric phase was first introduced by Pancharatnam
 in his study of interference of classical
light in distinct states of polarization. Berry 
discovered the quantal counterpart of Pancharatnam's phase in the case
of cyclic adiabatic evolution. Since then there has been an immense
interest in holonomy effects in quantum mechanics, which has led to
many generalizations of the notion of geometric phase. The extension
to nonadiabatic cyclic evolution was developed by Aharonov and Anandan
. Samuel and Bhandari generalized
the pure state geometric phase further by extending it to noncyclic
evolution and sequential projection measurements. The geometric phase
is a consequence of quantum kinematics and is thus independent of the
detailed nature of the dynamical origin of the path in state space.
This led Mukunda and Simon to put forward a kinematic
approach by taking the path traversed in state space as the primary
concept for the geometric phase. Further generalizations and
refinements, by relaxing the conditions of adiabaticity, unitarity,
and cyclicity of the evolution, have since been carried out
.Another line of development has been towards extending the geometric
phase to mixed states. This was first addressed by Uhlmann 
within the mathematical context of purification. Sjöqvist et al.
 introduced an alternative definition of geometric
phase for nondegenerate density operators based upon quantum
interferometry. Singh et al. gave a kinematic
description of the mixed state geometric phase in
Ref. and extended it to degenerate
density operators. The relation between phases of an entangled system
and its subsystems has been investigated . The concept
of off-diagonal geometric phases in Ref. for pure states
has also been generalized to mixed states undergoing unitary evolution
. Recently, the mixed state geometric phase
in Ref. has been verified experimentally using nuclear
magnetic resonance technique
.The generalization of the mixed state geometric phase to nonunitary
evolution has been addressed , .

input: What is the reason for exotic particles to necessitate hypercharge flux in F-theory GUTs?
expected_output: The reason for exotic particles to necessitate hypercharge flux in F-theory GUTs is that models with hypercharge flux GUT group breaking and singlets charged under Peccei-Quinn like gauge symmetries have been argued to require the presence of exotics in the spectrum. This is because the bosons associated with the extra U(1)s are in general anomalous and become massive in the usual way, leading to the necessity of exotic particles to cancel out these anomalies.
context:
Nevertheless, one can still achieve such breaking by means of an
additional flux {{formula:1bebedf5-ec2b-4157-b9db-fc5b97f03fad}} along the hypercharge generator in {{formula:02119fdf-ec46-4ac0-a3d8-9d3eadd44ac8}} , leading to the same symmetry breaking effect
as an adjoint Higgssing. Interestingly enough, this hypercharge flux is also a source for
doublet-triplet splitting of the Higgs multiplets {{formula:eb2c5cf6-bc11-45d4-b9c8-c53d87b9e08a}} .Besides the above points of {{formula:ef1685ce-0a58-4a69-945a-a8f1e1eca903}} and {{formula:793699af-2892-47d5-801b-537411f82ba5}} enhancement, F-theory {{formula:7b8b4f23-d660-46d4-b7b2-d4ff60bb83a5}} GUTs may also contain points at which the gauge symmetry is enhanced to {{formula:c4290d7a-fc8a-49f8-9408-6d3df76bf56b}} . These correspond to {{formula:f8b2ac02-e27b-4381-94bb-6ef0ec92bc71}} intersections between two 5-plet curves and a singlet curve, as can be derived from the adjoint branching
{{formula:f52c81b7-2a94-4fe2-af86-f9e9fa02f578}}The bosons associated to the extra {{formula:545a804c-0040-4b8a-b74f-6776e10fa1f9}} s are in general anomalous and become massive
in the usual way.F-theory models with hypercharge flux GUT group breaking and {{formula:45f537ad-ecb2-4170-96b8-2c5c962db790}} singlets charged under {{formula:e65bfa29-83dd-4fbb-87a2-468957fa3414}} Peccei-Quinn like gauge symmetries have been argued to require the presence of exotics in the spectrum, . Here we assume models with no exotics or with very massive ones. Other constructions, such as those where the singlets are not charged under the extra {{formula:2ff5b809-3e23-40f6-8a5d-3e45c46d17cf}} s (for instance, if they come from closed and/or open string moduli in the microscopic theory) also fit well within this context.The simplest models of this class contain one extra singlet {{formula:af83d2ed-5c7a-453b-8a45-e30ac4b74632}} coupling to the Higgs multiplets and at low energies are equivalent to the scale invariant NMSSM. In what follows we consider that specific setup. The structure of the superpotential is thus given by

Similar counting for the {{formula:e4cfd823-f8e9-48d4-8938-1b4906a448c1}} split, with the unique traceless {{formula:47a948d8-c7ca-43ae-9892-a4b7d0927601}} , implies a one-parameter flux configuration and this is given in table REF .
[Table: Table showing one-parameter family of hypercharge flux configurations compatible with anomalies for the case of a 3⊕2\left[3\oplus 2\right] split.]In particular note that this is incompatible with the naive doublet-triplet splitting configuration for the Higgs curve assignments determined by the Yukawa couplings in that the flux on the up-Higgs curve {{formula:ab85eb62-1739-4f96-b5cb-050541ed8457}} must vanish. Doublet-triplet splitting can be achieve in principle by coupling the Higgs triplet to a triplet on the matter curve and giving them a mass by an appropriate singlet vev that breaks the {{formula:ae13a1b8-ea56-4862-ae64-071630cb7c78}} , however this would also induce large R-parity violating terms.For the cases where there are multiple {{formula:e8e3ea3a-f523-4554-88ab-a159a4ae441c}} s present it is informative to do some parameter and constraint counting comparisons. Consider the case with no monodromies, then the constraint (REF ) must hold for the 4 traceless linearly independent {{formula:37044228-9082-44c4-823b-b242272f503a}} combinations. However we can also forget about the tracelessness constraint and take a basis of 5 {{formula:cc31d8b5-3ea6-498d-9697-179044602ca9}} s labeled by {{formula:ec995f6c-a6c3-4b10-b72a-6a3796f56b05}} and impose that (REF ) holds for all 5 of these {{formula:209d047e-2437-4ced-b035-3bc950081655}} s. Naively this would seem like over constraining, but if we consider the combination {{formula:34b421a7-9695-4002-8f52-1d705e83d775}} then (REF ) is automatically implied from (REF ). Hence we can consider a basis of {{formula:29bcdeb8-6e5a-4974-81cd-b7adc998d87c}} s given by the {{formula:c12d1b86-40f2-4967-9086-6d8d04c068b7}} . input: How do bounded expansion graph classes enable constant-factor approximations?
expected_output: Bounded expansion graph classes enable constant-factor approximations because they have a linear number of edges due to their average degree being bounded, which allows for efficient approximation algorithms. In these classes, every monotone maximization problem expressible in first-order logic admits a constant-factor approximation algorithm, even in the weighted setting. This is a result of the connection between approximability and the existence of algorithms parameterized by the solution size, where the existence of an EPTAS implies fixed-parameter tractability. The bounded expansion property of these graph classes provides a restrictive setting that facilitates the development of efficient approximation algorithms, making constant-factor approximations possible for various maximization problems.
context:
We are interested in approximation algorithms for problems such as the Maximum Independent Set
and its variants (weighted, distance-{{formula:916e7c0e-3172-4a82-89b0-4e8ab266d9e1}} independent for a fixed parameter {{formula:71495932-7620-46d9-a9ed-be7732d201cf}} , ...),
Maximum Induced Matching, Maximum 3-Colorable Induced Subgraph, and similar.
There are many strong non-approximation results that preclude the existence of constant-factor
approximation algorithms for these problems in general; for example, it is NP-hard to
approximate the independence number  of an {{formula:37d6d4cd-3b6d-4c81-abaf-ede992edfd47}} -vertex graph up to the factor of {{formula:a864de6f-37c6-4ba4-b782-e47d92e472fe}} for
every {{formula:0c8ae786-4199-4f57-ba5f-f528cd9a5939}} . Hence, we need to consider more restricted settings.There is a close connection between approximability and the existence of algorithms parameterized by the solution size.
Indeed, the existence of an EPTAS (arbitrarily precise polynomial-time approximation algorithm such that the degree
of the polynomial bounding the complexity does not depend on the precision) directly implies fixed-parameter tractability,
and a constant-factor approximation often forms a starting point for proving fixed-parameter tractability.
A natural family of problems, namely those expressible in the first-order logic, is known to be fixed-parameter tractable
in a subgraph-closed class of graphs if and (under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions) only if
the class is nowhere-dense . Moreover, in a slightly more restrictive setting of
classes with bounded expansion, the parameterized algorithms have linear time complexity .
We refer the reader not familiar with the concept of bounded expansion to Section REF ;
here, let us just mention that examples of graph classes with this property are
planar graphs and more generally all proper minor-closed classes, all graph
classes with bounded maximum degree, and even more generally, graph classes
closed under topological minors, as well as almost all Erdős-Rényi random
graphs with bounded average degree.Motivated by this connection, we explore the approximability of maximization problems expressible in the first-order logic
when restricted to classes with bounded expansion. As our first main result, we show that every monotone
maximization problems expressible in the first-order logic admits a constant-factor approximation algorithm
in every class of graphs of bounded expansion, even in the weighted setting. We need a few definitions to formulate the precise statement.Let {{formula:e873d8d0-6b14-4d2f-9cb1-eec494873626}} be a finite index set and let {{formula:da68a0fc-ebf3-4622-b9a3-13a4626e6108}} be a set of vertices of a graph {{formula:67252b68-eedb-4afb-8347-9c0fb8e181de}} .

Degeneracy at most {{formula:e4bd5121-27f2-491b-a280-882d4b587dcd}} 
implies that the graph and all its subgraphs have average degree at
most {{formula:c19320b3-0da0-4cc8-8979-52a0a7d06122}} and hence have a linear number of edges. Contrarily,
graphs in nowhere dense classes can have an edge density
of {{formula:b3fa5304-55a8-4f37-9906-1f4d9b325107}} and are therefore not necessarily degenerate.
“Nowhere density” turns out to be a very robust concept with several
seemingly unrelated natural characterisations (see
, ). Furthermore, Nešetřil and
Ossona de Mendez  established a clear-cut dichotomy
between nowhere dense and somewhere dense graph classes. The exact
definition of nowhere dense graph classes is
technical and we defer it to Section .
[Figure: Sparse graph classes]Theorem 1.1 
For every nowhere dense class {{formula:6ae0ce76-01d1-4ebe-bd2a-799862f09da2}} and every {{formula:aac85345-cdf7-4400-b33f-9ea7c0026eb7}} ,
every property of graphs definable in first-order logic can be
decided in time {{formula:c899514c-358a-4e60-a5d8-1b9c72cda2c6}} on {{formula:d7c93a9d-7ff3-45e6-b687-7b0695a0fed7}} .In particular, deciding first-order properties is fixed-parameter
tractable on nowhere dense graph classes.There is a minor
issue regarding non-uniform vs uniform fixed-parameter tractability,
see Remark REF . Deciding first-order properties of
arbitrary graphs is known to be complete for the parameterized
complexity class {{formula:fb074211-c598-4ce4-b118-da07871ff2a8}} and thus unlikely to be
fixed-parameter tractable .Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez already
proved that deciding properties definable in existential first-order
logic is fixed-parameter tractable on nowhere dense graphs. Dawar and
Kreutzer  showed that dominating set (parameterized
by the size of the solution) is fixed-parameter tractable on nowhere
dense graphs. Our theorem implies new fixed-parameter tractability
results on nowhere dense graphs for many other standard parameterized
problems, for example, connected dominating set and digraph kernel
(both parameterized by the size of the solution), Steiner tree
(parameterized by the size of the tree) and circuit satisfiability
(parameterized by the depth of the circuit and the Hamming weight of
the solution). The last result requires the generalisation of our
theorem from graphs to arbitrary relational structures, which is
straightforward.Our theorem can be seen as the culmination of a long line of meta
theorems for first order logic. The starting point is Seese's
 result that first-order properties of bounded degree
graphs can be decided in linear time. Frick and Grohe 
gave linear time algorithms for planar graphs and all apex-minor-free
graph classes and {{formula:e1a04129-9b13-4d68-a87a-0f8cf26845d4}} algorithms for graphs of
bounded local tree-width. Flum and Grohe  proved that
deciding first-order properties is fixed-parameter tractable on graph
classes with excluded minors, and Dawar, Grohe, and
Kreutzer  extended this to classes of graphs locally
excluding a minor.

input: How does PNS attack impact QKD security over long distances compared to short distances?
expected_output: The Photon-Number-Splitting (PNS) attack has a more significant impact on the security of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over long distances compared to short distances. This is because the channel transmittance decreases with distance, making it more likely for an eavesdropper, Eve, to intercept and measure a photon from a multi-photon pulse without introducing noise, thereby gaining information about the key. In long-distance QKD, the overall transmittance can be very low, on the order of 10^(-4) or even 10^(-6), which increases the vulnerability to PNS attacks. In contrast, over short distances, the channel transmittance is higher, reducing the effectiveness of PNS attacks and making QKD more secure. Therefore, to maintain security over long distances, it is essential to estimate the fraction of tagged bits in Bob's raw key and use techniques such as the ILM-GLLP model to distill a secure final key.
context:
One form of a CV quantum system is that represented by {{formula:bd481ca0-27e6-41bd-96fa-5bee5d76e32d}} bosonic modes, such as those corresponding to {{formula:24c5ed79-62bb-4359-9dd5-6eb9efd63d00}} quantized radiation modes of the electromagnetic field, . A single photon has four degrees of freedom, helicity (polarization) and the three components of the momentum vector. In principle, quantum information can be encoded into any one of these degrees of freedom. A single `mode' of an electromagnetic field refers to a specific combination of these photonic degrees of freedom. In many circumstances different modes can be simply represented by different frequencies (since frequency is related to momentum). For a beam of photons, the number of photons in the beam constitutes another means to encode quantum information. Quantum information encoded into the quadratures of the electromagnetic field (formally defined below) are related to an encoding in this additional degree of freedom. Since the quadrature operators have continuous spectra, we can describe the values of such operators as CV variables.A single mode of a CV system can be described as a single quantum harmonic oscillator of a specific frequency, where the electric and magnetic fields play the `roles' of the position and momentum . It will be useful to further illustrate this concept.
Consider the case of a single-frequency radiation field confined to a one-dimensional cavity with walls that are perfectly conducting. Assume the {{formula:24639a9c-72a7-4704-9f23-439ed058e628}} -axis is parallel to the length of the cavity and the cavity walls are located at {{formula:bddabae5-2b38-4124-96ca-d7b528bffa42}} and {{formula:5c5376b2-2847-4cc1-935d-101aecafca49}} . The electric field within the cavity will form a standing wave. Without loss of generality, we can take the electric field to be polarized perpendicular to the {{formula:264b6920-889d-44ae-a16f-2568998307f7}} -axis, and in the positive {{formula:6062075a-492a-478f-8a12-2c54a2744372}} -direction (we take the {{formula:d676fc9f-615d-477d-90d7-5670cbb71614}} and {{formula:bd593cbd-c058-4b2a-9c7d-c991e83bc8a4}} coordinates to be in same plane and the {{formula:727c8e7e-9971-4bad-b2d1-5315c5702c59}} plane perpendicular to the {{formula:fa33b966-9359-46ef-967a-de8e4ff7d273}} plane). In terms of the distance vector r and time {{formula:f0753ee8-a786-455e-9828-fa192d517803}} , the electric field can then be written as {{formula:c9884912-f581-42e5-b51f-bd107bc41b64}} , where {{formula:4086a175-8f7b-4613-9519-b389d4182417}} is a unit-length polarization vector.

In practice, the channel can be very lossy. For example, if we want
to do QKD over a distance longer than 100 km using an optical fiber
and the light pulses of wavelength 1.55 {{formula:bb69c30f-bc5f-42f8-ae86-2b9f1ab11550}} , the overall
transmittance can be in the magnitude order of {{formula:9fc3e6b0-a13e-49b2-9e1e-136a55fbb464}} or even
{{formula:3b17fb1a-c4a5-41c5-94e8-89b0d31d6161}} . (Suppose the detection efficiency is around 10%.) This
opens a door for the Eve by the so called photon-number-splitting
(PNS) attack, 
as shown
in figure (REF ). Suppose at a certain time Alice sends out a
multi-photon pulse. Every photon inside the same pulse is in the
same state in coding space, e.g., the polarization space. Eve can
keep one photon from the pulse and sends other photons of the pulse
to Bob through a transparent channel. This action will not cause any
noise in the coding space but Eve may have full information about
Bob's bit: After the measurement basis is announced by Alice or Bob,
Eve will be always able to measure the photon she has kept in the
correct basis. Therefore, here we regard all those bits caused by
multi-photon pulses from Alice as the tagged bits. According
to the model given by ILM-GLLP as we have studied, if the
fraction of tagged bits in Bob's raw key is not too large, we can
still obtain a secure final key by equation (REF ). In using
this result, we must first know the value {{formula:6e8b358e-9c04-4e80-88d3-5567bef94919}} .
Alice does not know which pulse contains more than one photons, she
only knows a distribution over different photon numbers for all
pulses. As we have mentioned, the fraction of multi-photon pulses
from the source can be very different from the fraction of
tagged bits in Bob's raw key, for, Eve's channel transmittance can
be dependent on the photon number of the pulse from Alice. Naively,
one can assume the worst case to estimate {{formula:073b34ce-90c0-4720-aeee-26d9e4bd6603}} : the channel
transmittance for multi-photon pulses is 1 and we check how many raw
bits are generated. If the number is larger than the number of
multi-photon pulses, there must be some untagged bits. However, in
such a way, the light intensity must be rather weak in order to
have some untagged bits. Suppose the channel transmittance is {{formula:60afc529-1677-4d04-b85b-1d132f1668a0}} 
and the light pulse intensity is {{formula:102796ee-074c-4e4c-92c2-89753e48721b}} . The density operator of a
phased randomized coherent state of intensity {{formula:b1624311-0508-4c0d-80fa-d93437c50eb3}} is
{{formula:6dfbbc30-2f41-4333-8e6d-0227e969438a}}Consider the normal case that there is no Eve, the channel
transmittance is {{formula:c541aa93-4326-48c6-8a67-d96f39c3683a}} to every photon.

input: What are the advantages of using a larger patch size to enhance semantic information capture in deep learning models?
expected_output: Using a larger patch size in deep learning models has several advantages, particularly in enhancing the capture of semantic information. A larger patch size provides an enlarged receptive field, which allows the network to capture more semantic information. This is especially beneficial when training a deeper network, as it enables the model to take full advantage of the increased capacity. Additionally, a larger patch size can lead to improved performance, with the deeper model achieving more significant improvement in terms of PSNR, such as 0.12dB, compared to the shallower model, which achieves 0.04dB. However, it is worth noting that using a larger patch size also increases training time and consumes more computing resources, requiring a trade-off between performance and computational efficiency.
context: Our training process is divided into two stages, namely a warm-up stage and then the main stage. First, we trained only the generators by using the {{formula:7940d6f8-eca6-4a2c-adb3-d031411396a5}} for 10 epochs. We used the initialization method mentioned in , using a smaller initialization for ease of training a very deep network. The trained model at the warm-up stage was used as an initialization for the main stage. This {{formula:4d4a3c7b-bbb1-4fe8-92da-4aa3f631866d}} -oriented pre-trained model provides a reasonable initial point for training GANs, for which a balance between quantitative accuracy of the reconstruction and visual quality of the output is required. For the main stage, we trained the generators alternately with the discriminators for 100 epochs. We used Adam with momentum 0.5 for both stages. The initial learning rates for generators and discriminators were set to 0.0001 and 0.0004 respectively. We trained them for 10 epochs with the initial rates and linearly decayed the rates to zero over the last 90 epochs. The hyper-parameters of the loss terms in Eq. (1) and Eq. (7) were set to {{formula:9ce2c96f-f385-42ec-adf8-a3c49cf17ef6}} = 5.0, {{formula:d481e060-9e6c-41ce-8f25-3955a538ce61}} = 0.001, {{formula:a3c1da02-d36f-4f93-8b04-3ff365be3cb6}} = 0.05, {{formula:8e196123-7c36-4748-af9f-9561d72d83ff}} = 80.0, and {{formula:3b7597c3-03dd-4e7e-8e1c-6c2ab6014a89}} = 0.1. We developed our model using Pytorch 1.5.0 and trained it on two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080Ti GPUs.

We observe that training a deeper network benefits from a larger patch size, since an enlarged receptive field helps
the network to capture more semantic information.
We try training patch size {{formula:4efdc89b-bf3e-42ce-a506-d3763d546d79}} , {{formula:a3492d8f-3666-445e-b061-c06caa91fc37}} and {{formula:292b3880-20d2-4730-a1c8-5e90542086f8}} on models with 16 RBs and 23 RRDBs (larger
model capacity). The training curves (evaluated on Set5 with RGB channels) are shown in Fig. REF .It is observed that both models benefit from larger training patch size.
Moreover, the deeper model achieves more improvement ({{formula:6751be9b-e8de-4dd9-9d22-74a42ce8356f}} 0.12dB) than the shallower one ({{formula:0e768c8e-d491-43f0-a70e-8677ecca118d}} 0.04dB) since
larger model capacity is capable of taking full advantage of larger training patch size.However, larger training patch size costs more training time and consumes more computing resources.
As a trade-off, we use {{formula:3a9ede26-054e-4b55-b0df-ea525b4ca8dd}} for PSNR-oriented methods and {{formula:b5fb1bda-3590-44a6-9b80-bcf0b873be69}} for perceptual-driven methods.
[Figure: The influence of training patch size (PSNR is evaluated on Set5 with RGB channels).]

input: What impact do activation functions and optimization algorithms have on the ability of Deep Neural Networks to solve 3D Partial Differential Equations?
expected_output: The activation functions and optimization algorithms have a significant impact on the ability of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to solve 3D Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). The choice of activation functions allows neural networks to be applied to many nonlinear models, enabling them to learn complex patterns in the data. Optimization algorithms, on the other hand, play a crucial role in updating model parameters and minimizing the loss function, which is essential for achieving accurate solutions. In the context of solving 3D PDEs, the selection of optimal configuration of the neural network, including the activation functions and optimization algorithms, is critical to obtaining the best possible solution. For instance, the use of the sigmoid activation function and the Quasi-Newton BFGS optimization method has been shown to perform well in solving certain types of PDEs. Therefore, careful consideration of these factors is necessary to fully leverage the potential of DNNs in solving complex 3D PDEs.
context:
They were also adopted to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), but shallow ANNs are unable to learn the complex nonlinear patterns effectively. With improved theories incorporating unsupervised pre-training, stacks of auto-encoder variants, and deep belief nets, deep learning has become also an interesting alternative to classical methods such as FEM.According to the universal approximation theorem, any continuous function can be approximated by a feedforward neural network with one single hidden layer. However, the number of neurons of the hidden layer tends to increase exponentially with increasing complexity and non-linearity of a model. Recent studies show that DNNs render better approximations for nonlinear functions . Some researchers employed deep learning for the solution of PDEs. E et al. developed a deep learning-based numerical method for high-dimensional parabolic PDEs and back-forward stochastic differential equations , . Raissi et al. introduced physics-informed neural networks for supervised learning of nonlinear partial differential equations. Beck et al. employed deep learning to solve nonlinear stochastic differential equations and Kolmogorov equations. Sirignano and Spiliopoulos provided a theoretical proof for deep neural networks as PDE approximators, and concluded that it converged as the number of hidden layers tend to infinity. Anitescu et al. , Guo et al. , and Nguyen-Thanh et al. applied deep neural networks for finding the solutions for second and fourth order boundary value problems.In practice the learning ability of deep neural networks can strongly rely on the using of the configurations of the neural network and the optimization algorithms. Such as the activation functions, optimization algorithms, with the activation functions the neural networks can be applied to many nonlinear models, and optimization algorithms can update model parameters and minimize the value of the loss function. In this paper, we therefore compare the different parameters to select the optimal configuration of the neural network. In this context, We use deep learning method to get the optimal solution of the three dimensional problems.The paper is organised as follows:
First, we describe the three dimensional problems of potential in-homogeneous media. Then we introduce the deep learning based collocation method, which includes the neural network architecture, activation function, sampling method and a convergence proof. Subsequently, the results of numerical tests are presented. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the deep learning method for solving problems of potential in non-homogeneous media.

In this section we report on the solution of a number of model problems.
In all cases we used a multilayer perceptron having one hidden layer
with 10 hidden units and one linear output unit. The sigmoid activation of each
hidden unit is {{formula:cebb23ba-58ad-457c-9b77-f6dd08e7f6ec}} .
For each test problem the exact analytic solution {{formula:4e0b6f77-9043-435b-9f42-2f0055d64996}} 
was known in advance. Therefore we test the accuracy of the obtained
solutions by computing the deviation {{formula:7d13deef-2a76-41a4-985b-7bda528f5dae}} .
To perform the error minimization we employed the Merlin
, optimization package. Merlin provides an
environment for multidimensional continuous function optimization.
From the several algorithms that are implemented therein, the
Quasi–Newton BFGS method seemed to perform better
in these kind of problems and hence we used it in all of our experiments.
A simple criterion for the gradient norm was used for termination.In order to illustrate the
characteristics of the solutions provided by the neural
method, we provide figures displaying the corresponding deviation
{{formula:3aa95fd7-3eb1-4e88-8e1c-e29f5e7866b0}} 
both at the few points (training points)
that were used for training and at many other points (test points) of
the domain of each equation. The second kind of figures are of major importance
since they show the interpolation capabilities of the neural
solutions which seem
to be superior compared
to other solutions. Moreover, in the case of ODEs we also
consider points outside the training interval in order to obtain an estimate
of the extrapolation performance of the obtained solution.

input: Can dual meshes actually enhance the accuracy of shear stress calculations in complex simulations?
expected_output: The use of dual meshes in simulating erosion can indeed enhance the accuracy of shear stress calculations in complex simulations. By discretizing the boundary of the geometry at a set of collocation points distributed equally in arclength, the integral equation can be solved more accurately, which in turn leads to more precise calculations of shear stress. Additionally, the application of different quadrature rules, such as the trapezoid rule or the Barycentric quadrature rule, depending on the proximity of the target point to the source points, can further improve the accuracy of the calculations. This approach allows for a more detailed and accurate representation of the complex interactions between the fluid and the bodies, ultimately leading to more reliable results in simulations involving erosion and shear stress.
context:
In line with our previous work , we use two meshes to
simulate erosion. The integral equation is solved by discretizing the
boundary of the geometry at a set of collocation points distributed
equally in arclength (section REF ).
Depending on the proximity of the target point to the source points, the
quadrature rule is either the trapezoid rule or the Barycentric
quadrature rule (section REF ). The criteria that determines
which quadrature method is applied is described in
section REF . Once the shear stress is computed, the bodies
are eroded a single time step by using a {{formula:419dbe42-efc1-4159-b231-1c37c06be81d}} –{{formula:bd3b8646-aa55-45d2-baf4-8343035e000f}} 
discretization , . The time
stepping methods for erosion and passive particles are described in
section REF .

A scaling constant often appears in the erosion model in (REF ), but in the Stokes limit, the constant only sets the time scale, so we have taken it to be one. For the sake of numerical stability, we will modify the erosion model in Section REF .The outer wall is formed by rounding off the corners of {{formula:d68274b4-5ae1-4662-b09e-519ecb1846df}} , and we impose the Hagen-Poiseuille flow
{{formula:fbc4895a-3bb8-42dd-b0ca-39e31b1f5bd2}}where {{formula:759f7ffb-df7d-4c24-9f67-d3eff47a8398}} sets the maximum of the imposed Poiseuille flow. Often, we will simply set {{formula:5cd652db-9468-4a79-b5f6-85cc22d2fa8e}} , but in some instances we change {{formula:4686b7c1-85a0-4225-9d29-4a32cc11fa4b}} dynamically to enforce that the pressure drop across the computational cell is constant as bodies erode within it. To minimize the boundary effects of the inflow and outflow, we only place bodies in the center third, {{formula:4f416bae-1c44-41ea-aec2-bb415eca9150}} , of the fluid domain.
[Figure: A schematic for the governing equations. A no-slip boundary condition is imposed on each body γ ℓ \gamma _\ell whose unit normal points outward relative to the geometry. On the outer geometry Γ\Gamma , a Hagen-Poiseuille flow is imposed. The bodies erode at a rate that is equal to the magnitude of the shear stress applied by the fluid. The bodies are constrained to the middle third of the channel that is located between the dashed lines.]We describe how the incompressible Stokes equations are solved in {{formula:09c1570c-e340-454c-8139-7defbd9b0a42}} using a boundary integral equation in Section REF . In Section REF , we discuss how the shear stress is computed. Finally, in Section REF , we describe how corners in the bodies are avoided and perform a change of coordinates to treat a stiff term.

input: What causes model biases when trained on unverified web texts in OSCAR?
expected_output: The model biases when trained on unverified web texts in OSCAR are caused by the presence of explicit and indecent material, unverified information, and commonly found lies and misconceptions, which can lead to a skewed model that reflects gender, racial, and religious biases found in textual data of all registers.
context:
We have available to us, a range of different German language corpora that we use in different combinations for our model pretraining. OSCAR is a set of monolingual corpora extracted from Common Crawl. The Common Crawl texts are pre-processed (e.g. HTML entities are removed) and a language classification model is used to sort texts by language. We use the unshuffled version of the German OSCAR corpus, resulting in 145GB of text. The Wikipedia dump for German is preprocessed with the WikiExtractorhttps://github.com/attardi/wikiextractor script forming a corpus of size 6GB. The OPUS projecthttp://opus.nlpl.eu has collected texts from various domains such as movie subtitles, parliament speeches and books and these comprise a collection of around 10GB. From Open Legal Datahttp://openlegaldata.io/research/2019/02/19/court-decision-dataset.html there is a dataset of about 2.4GB of German court decisions. Table REF shows an overview over all datasets.As discussed in Section , our pretrained language models will learn pre-existing biases from the training datasets. The main portion (89%) of our training data, namely the OSCAR dataset, uses texts scraped from the internet, which is in some respects problematic. First off, this dataset contains a lot of explicit and indecent material. While we filtered out many of these documents through keyword matching, we cannot guarantee that this method was successful in every case. Furthermore, many websites contain unverified information and any dataset containing this kind of text can lead to a skewed model that reflects commonly found lies and misconceptions. This includes gender, racial and religious biases which are found in textual data of all registers and so we advise that anyone using our model to recognise that it will not always build true and accurate representation of real world concepts. We implore users of the model to seriously consider these issues before deploying it in a production setting, especially in situations where impartiality matter, such as journalism, and institutional decision making like job applications or insurance assessments.
[Table: The size of each dataset in gigabytes.]

In conclusion, we see the Open Legal Data Platform as an important first step towards openness in the legal domain that will ultimately enable more collaboration among researchers and improve access to justice for the general public.
In this context, we consider the MediaWiki software as role model, that powers all Wikipedias and helped to make encyclopedic knowledge available, and envision to achieve something comparable but for the legal domain.
Making data technically open and accessible is only the beginning.
In the future, we will also focus on Legal Design in order to make the data and information useful and usable not only for professional users, but also understandable and actionable for lay people.
The research presented in this article is funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) through the project Software-Sprint (grant no. 01IS16021).

input: What are the properties of local minima statistics in random graphs and how do they relate to the formation of Corrugated Surfaces?
expected_output: The properties of local minima statistics in random graphs are related to the formation of Corrugated Surfaces, which are configurations that maximize the packing of local minima. The study of local minima statistics in random landscapes defined on graphs is a general problem that arises in various fields, including the study of a point particle in a random potential and the energy landscape of many-body systems. Research has shown that the probability of large deviations, such as configurations with maximally packed local minima, can be addressed through analytical and numerical estimates. Specifically, the constant that controls the number of such configurations in the limit of large system size has been estimated for Cayley trees and hypercubic lattices. Furthermore, the Permutation Generated Random Walk has been defined to study the statistical properties of these configurations, including the distribution of end-to-end distance, intermediate points, and correlation functions. The connection between the one-dimensional ballistic deposition process and dynamics on permutations has also been established, allowing for the reconstruction of the probability distribution of having a certain number of peaks in the uniform ballistic deposition process. Overall, the study of local minima statistics in random graphs provides insight into the formation of Corrugated Surfaces and the behavior of complex systems.

input: How do REPRESSURED codes compare to Steiner codes in terms of flexibility and repetition tradeoffs?
expected_output: REPRESSURED codes offer greater flexibility and repetition tradeoffs compared to Steiner codes due to their resolvable nature, which allows for a natural tradeoff between the repetition degree and the number of parallel classes. This means that REPRESSURED codes can be constructed to have higher or lower repetition degrees simply by including or removing parallel classes, whereas Steiner codes require the use of the entire system and may not be resolvable. Additionally, REPRESSURED codes can provide examples of fractional repetition codes with parameters that are not covered by Steiner systems, addressing an open question in previous work. Overall, the flexibility and tradeoffs of REPRESSURED codes make them a more versatile and adaptable option for distributed storage systems.

input: How can the uncertainty principle be applied to calculate the relation between Δx and Δp in quantum mechanics?
expected_output: The uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics can be applied to calculate the relation between Δx and Δp by using the uncertainty relation formula, which states that the product of the uncertainty in position (Δx) and the uncertainty in momentum (Δp) is greater than or equal to a constant value. In the context of a lattice with nearest neighbor hopping only, the uncertainty relation can be calculated as Δx * Δp >= ħ/2, where ħ is the reduced Planck constant. This relation indicates that as the uncertainty in position decreases, the uncertainty in momentum increases, and vice versa. Furthermore, the uncertainty relation for a lattice can be expressed as Δx = sqrt(ħ^2 / (4 * m^2)) * sqrt(1 + (m * t)^2), where m is the mass of the particle and t is time. The uncertainty in momentum is the same as in the continuum limit, given by Δp = ħ / Δx. Consequently, the uncertainty relation for this case on a lattice is Δx * Δp >= ħ/2, which demonstrates that the uncertainty never decreases as a function of time, with the degree of increase depending on the mean momentum.

input: What are the advantages of using complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in Lie superalgebra analysis?
expected_output: The use of complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in Lie superalgebra analysis provides several advantages, including the ability to deal with degree of membership and nonmembership in the complex plane, making the concept more effective and useful in scientific fields. Additionally, complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets allow for the generalization of fuzzy sets and intuitionistic fuzzy sets, enabling the study of more complex and nuanced relationships between elements in Lie superalgebras. The application of complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in Lie superalgebra analysis also enables the investigation of properties such as complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals, which can provide valuable insights into the structure and behavior of Lie superalgebras. Furthermore, the use of complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in decision-making problems, as generalized by Garg and Rani, can facilitate more informed and accurate decision-making in complex systems. Overall, the advantages of using complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in Lie superalgebra analysis lie in their ability to capture and analyze complex relationships and uncertainties in a more comprehensive and effective manner.

In this article, we define the complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals of Lie superalgebras. input: What insights does Berry phase theory provide into the properties of topological ferromagnets?
expected_output: Berry phase theory provides significant insights into the properties of topological ferromagnets, particularly in understanding the role of nontrivial topology in enhancing orbital magnetization. The theory reveals that a nontrivial real-space distribution of spins can lead to a finite topological orbital magnetization, even in the absence of spin-orbit interaction. This is evident from the fact that the peak value of the total orbital magnetization is larger in systems with nontrivial topology, such as Chern insulators, compared to those without. Furthermore, the modern theory of orbital magnetization, which incorporates Berry phase theory, is crucial for describing magnetism in topological orbital ferromagnets, as it goes beyond the limitations of the atom-centered approximation. By accounting for the integrated Berry curvature, the theory provides a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the orbital magnetization in these materials, highlighting the importance of topology in determining their magnetic properties.

75.30.-m, 75.70.Ak, 73.43.-fMagnetism is an elementary property of materials, and it is composed of spin and orbital contributions. In contrast to the concept of spin magnetization, which has been relatively well understood and extensively researched in the course of the past decades, our understanding of orbital magnetism in solids has been poor so far, and an ability to describe it reliably has been missing until recently. Both spin and orbital magnetization (OM) are accessible separately, e.g., by means of magnetomechanical  or magnetic circular dichroism measurements, but the orbital contribution to the magnetization of solids is usually overshadowed by the spin counterpart, owing to the orbital moment quenching. However, in certain systems the OM yields an equally important contribution, which can even result in a spin-orbital compensation of magnetization, . Its influence on spin-dependent transport, magnetic susceptibility , orbital magnetoelectric response, magnetic anisotropy , and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction  renders the OM crucial for understanding basic properties of magnets.
A spontaneous OM in ferromagnets is a key manifestation of the spin-orbit interaction (SOI), lifting in part the quenching mechanism. This interpretation applies to most materials but it fails to explain orbital magnetism in systems where a finite topological OM emerges even without SOI as a result of a nontrivial real-space distribution of spins .Addressing the OM in solids is a subtle point as the position operator {{formula:3694c00d-1f60-46b3-b559-e2cbbc21ff04}} is ill-defined in the basis of extended Bloch states. To circumvent this problem in ab initio calculations, the evaluation of the angular momentum operator {{formula:3d7b73ff-ceea-4881-b054-f4fac4be2255}} is typically restricted locally in space to atom-centered spheres. This atom-centered approximation (ACA) is widely used to study orbital magnetism in solids even nowadays. input: Does Khovanskii-Pukhlikov theory provide a valid approach to understanding the cohomology of torus manifolds?
expected_output: Khovanskii-Pukhlikov theory does provide a valid approach to understanding the cohomology of torus manifolds, as it allows for the description of the cohomology ring of a torus manifold using a construction known in toric varieties theory. This theory enables the definition of a homogeneous degree polynomial that represents the volume of corresponding virtual polyhedra, which is essential in understanding the cohomology of torus manifolds. Furthermore, the intersection number of sections of characteristic linear bundles on a torus manifold can be expressed in terms of the mixed volume of the corresponding virtual polyhedra, generalizing the BKK-theorem for torus manifolds. Additionally, the cohomology ring of a bundle with torus manifold fibers can be described in terms of integrals of polynomials over virtual polyhedra, demonstrating the applicability of Khovanskii-Pukhlikov theory to the study of torus manifolds.

input: What causes TFP-QPSK to achieve a higher spectral efficiency gain over other formats at long distances, and how do link nonlinear effects contribute to this outcome?
expected_output: TFP-QPSK achieves a higher spectral efficiency gain over other formats at long distances due to its ability to mitigate the effects of link nonlinearities. As the distance increases, link nonlinear effects significantly affect signal propagation, and TFP-QPSK is better suited to handle these effects. The use of linear modulation and optical filtering in TFP-QPSK helps to reduce the impact of nonlinearities, resulting in a higher spectral efficiency gain compared to other formats. In particular, the linearity of the modulator is preserved by employing a driving voltage significantly lower than the modulator half-wave voltage, which reduces the introduction of nonlinear interference. Additionally, the use of optical filtering helps to shape the pulse and reduce the effects of nonlinearities, allowing TFP-QPSK to outperform other systems at higher distances. Overall, the combination of linear modulation and optical filtering in TFP-QPSK enables it to achieve a higher spectral efficiency gain over other formats at long distances, where link nonlinear effects are more pronounced.

carriers, transmitted through the optical link, extracted by an optical
demultiplexer, and independently detected. In each transmitter, the
in-phase and quadrature components of two orthogonal states of polarization
are independently and linearly modulated by a pair of nested Mach-Zehnder
modulators (MZMs). In principle, the desired pulse shape {{formula:7324ec47-8494-4191-87b7-ac5bb58d4a99}} can
be obtained either operating on the electrical signals that drive
the modulator (through a low-pass filter (LPF), as actually shown
in the scheme of Fig. REF ) or on the optical signal after
the modulator (through an optical band-pass filter), provided that
the overall equivalent low-pass impulse response of the transmitter
(driver, modulator, electrical filter and/or optical filter) is {{formula:e9beaeb3-0936-4fe9-a9c1-578bd6feedaf}} 
and that linearity of the modulator is preserved by employing a driving
voltage significantly lower than the modulator half-wave voltage {{formula:1f4cbc3e-b571-44de-8811-9b75f5e31079}} .
A comparison of the performance obtained by optical or electrical
filtering when employing different driving voltages is presented in
. An alternative modulation scheme,
where linear modulation (REF ) is obtained by operating
the MZM at its maximum driving voltage (to reduce its insertion loss),
may also be devised. For instance, by using an additional MZM as a
pulse carver and employing optical filtering to obtain the desired
pulse shape {{formula:c67254da-f16b-428a-ba5c-65fd4fdf3894}} and {{formula:1a9ca7f9-88b3-4436-a69c-76cad9eac851}} product,
the nonlinearity of the MZM affects only (and slightly) the overall
pulse shape {{formula:e4e501a6-ee88-4a59-9ae3-219855bffbf5}} , but does not introduce nonlinear ISI. In this
scheme, however, the insertion loss saved by increasing the MZM driving
voltage is replaced by the additional loss introduced by the pulse
carver and optical filter. Finally, a possible implementation based
on an arrayed waveguide grating device that filters and multiplexes
all the frequency subchannels in the optical domain has been proposed
in . In this work, we consider a modulation
scheme based on a single MZM (driven at low voltage) and analogue
electrical filtering which, at the present, seems to be the most practical
choice in terms of cost and complexity.

input: How do architecture, training data, and optimizer choice impact CNN performance?
expected_output: The architecture, training data, and optimizer choice have a significant impact on the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). In the context of the experiments, two different CNN architectures, ResNet34 and VGG16, were used, and the results showed that the choice of architecture can affect the performance of the model. The training data also played a crucial role, as the models were first trained on non-incipient disease data and then fine-tuned on the full dataset, which helped to improve the performance. The optimizer choice also had an impact, as the Adam optimizer was used, which adapted the learning rate scale for different layers, resulting in faster convergence compared to other optimizers like Adagrad. Additionally, the use of pre-trained models and data augmentation techniques also contributed to the improved performance of the CNNs. Overall, the combination of architecture, training data, and optimizer choice can significantly impact the performance of CNNs, and careful selection of these factors is essential to achieve optimal results.
context: We used CNN models for classifying image models in the DR dataset. The CNN models were implemented using pytorch . The deep learning models used to construct our ensembles vary in their architecture, image data resolution, training set selection, number of training epochs and data augmentation strengths. Two different CNN architectures, ResNet34  and VGG16 , were used in our experiments. We used the binary-crossentropy loss function and the Adam  optimizer during training. All network parameters were initialized with the weights from pretrained models provided by the torchvision  package that were created for classifying objects from the ImageNet database.Since our experiments involved scanning various {{formula:4d91782e-900c-43d9-bf6e-9d9b4f5df8d5}} values, to reduce the total training effort, we first trained our models with non-incipient disease data (only SL0 & SL3 & SL4) for 130 epochs, and then continued to train the resulting networks with all training data (SL0 to SL4) till convergence. Most trained models reached an AUC of above {{formula:4a0308df-9211-4141-93de-c168f2b2b0fe}} on both the training and the validation sets. We discarded the bad performing models and put the rest into a pool. The retained models in the pool were then used as base learners for constructing ensembles. To create an ensemble model instance, we randomly picked {{formula:78478ad2-2a0b-4ae0-8491-992c1f74dcc8}} single learners from the pool. In our experiment, we evaluated {{formula:e912997b-2223-475e-8be4-20d229ec2f87}} and {{formula:9ec9ffd0-e069-4493-8bf7-86328a935c3c}} , two ensemble sizes used in previous works , . Their individual predictions were then combined and grouped for later analysis.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with several layers of convolution,
pooling and non-linear units have shown considerable success in computer vision
tasks. Unlike most fully connected neural nets, weight sharing in CNNs results
in vastly different gradients in different layers. A smaller learning rate for
the convolution layers is often used in practice when applying SGD. We show the
effectiveness of Adam in deep CNNs. Our CNN architecture has three alternating
stages of 5x5 convolution filters and 3x3 max pooling with stride of 2 that are
followed by a fully connected layer of 1000 rectified linear hidden units (ReLU's). The input image are pre-processed by whitening, and dropout noise is applied to the input layer and fully connected layer. The minibatch size is also set to 128 similar to previous experiments.Interestingly, although both Adam and Adagrad make rapid progress lowering the cost in the initial
stage of the training, shown in Figure REF (left), Adam and SGD
eventually converge considerably faster than Adagrad for CNNs shown in Figure
REF (right). We notice the second moment estimate
{{formula:30e016be-b671-4876-98bc-03b574da9c8a}} vanishes to zeros after a few epochs and is dominated by the {{formula:b7673a4d-192a-4f57-8811-3b5545f63db2}} in
algorithm . The second moment estimate is therefore a poor
approximation to the geometry of the cost function in CNNs comparing to fully
connected network from Section REF . Whereas, reducing the minibatch
variance through the first moment is more important in CNNs and contributes to
the speed-up. As a result, Adagrad converges much slower than others in this particular experiment. Though Adam shows marginal improvement over SGD with momentum, it
adapts learning rate scale for different layers instead of hand picking
manually as in SGD.

input: How does Frequency Modulation (FM) compare to Amplitude Modulation (AM) in terms of noise reduction capabilities in Spin Transfer Nano Oscillators (STNOs)?
expected_output: Frequency modulation usually offers an ideal method to reduce noise in communications, making it a preferable choice over amplitude modulation in terms of noise reduction capabilities in Spin Transfer Nano Oscillators (STNOs). However, in STNOs, the frequency and amplitude of the oscillatory signals are nonlinearly connected, which can affect the performance of frequency modulation. In contrast, pulse amplitude modulation provides a case where frequency and amplitude are uncoupled, allowing for a simpler modulation system, but it has a dissipative nature due to spin wave diffusion. Overall, frequency modulation is generally more effective in reducing noise, but its implementation in STNOs requires careful consideration of the nonlinear relationships between frequency and amplitude.
context:
STNO are spin-wave sources and detectors; their, radiating oscillatory signals may be modulated. Frequency modulation usually offers an ideal method to reduce noise in communications. However, the frequency and the amplitude of the oscillatory signals in STNO depend on the driving current; amplitude and frequency are nonlinearly connected. Experiments have shown the effect of nonlinear frequency modulation in single , and double STNO and the effect has been described theoretically in , .Pulse amplitude modulation provides a case where frequency and amplitude are uncoupled; turning the spin-wave sources on and off causes a spin-wave diffusive front to propagate away from the contacts every time the STNO are pulsed. In it was shown that pulse modulation of an STNO source has a dissipative nature because of the spin wave diffusion (see, Eq. REF ). However, information can still be processed and transmitted using a simple amplitude modulation system .Phase modulation may also be possible in STNO. Whenever a STNO phase locks to another STNO or to an external oscillatory signal, there is an interval of nominal frequencies where the STNO still synchronizes to the reference signal, . Within this frequency interval oscillators remain synchronized but their relative phase to the reference signal changes.
In most of the spectroscopic techniques one measures the phase difference between an external signal{{formula:14880296-bb89-453a-af5d-40eeeac088e9}} used to excite an intrinsic resonance{{formula:a18cba4e-7d9e-4ada-9938-afd8383da6c9}} and the intrinsic resonance (e.g., Ferromagnetic resonance). One may combine arrays of synchronized STNO and tune independently their relative phases with respect of an external signal. Phase modulation may provide an interesting option for encoding information as its detection is usually simple with the help of a reference signal.
